text:
The perfect gift for cats doesn't exist.

Every person who has ever loved one knows this in their bones. You stand in the pet aisle holding a feather wand, a catnip banana, a tunnel, a laser, a tiny fake mouse that cost more than your lunch. You bring it home. The cat inspects it for four seconds, delivers a verdict, and walks directly into the cardboard box it came in.

The box wins. The box always wins.

Cats are the toughest audience on earth, and they don't even have to say anything to prove it. A dog will pretend to love your gift. A dog will love your gift out of pure loyalty, even if it's a sock. A cat has no such courtesy. A cat will look you in the eye, look at the thing you spent money on, and slowly, deliberately, turn away.

That's the problem this post is about. And it's about the one object in a very long time that made me stop and ask whether the problem was ever the cat.

Because here's what I realized somewhere between the fifth abandoned toy and the sixth: we've been shopping for the wrong thing.

We shop for entertainment. Cats mostly ask for something else.

Stay with me for a minute. This gets stranger, and a lot more tender, than a gift guide has any right to be.

Start with the money, because the money tells the truth.

Americans spend well north of 140 billion dollars a year on their pets. Not in a decade. Every year. A big slice of that goes to toys, treats, beds, gadgets, fountains, scratching towers, cameras that let you watch your cat ignore the other things you bought. The industry has a shelf for every guilty feeling a person can have while leaving the house in the morning.

And yet ask any cat owner what their cat actually uses, and the answers come back almost embarrassingly small. The sunny spot on the floor. The one blanket that smells like them. The lap, if the lap is available and the cat has decided it is.

Warmth. A familiar smell. Someone close by.

That's it. That's the whole wishlist.

The billion-dollar aisle is built on the assumption that a bored cat needs stimulation. Sometimes that's true. But a lot of what looks like boredom in a cat is something quieter: a small animal in a large, silent room, waiting for the part of the day that has company in it.

So the real question for a gift-giver isn't "what will keep my cat busy?"

It's "what would make the empty hours feel less empty?"

And that question has a stranger answer than a toy.

Go back to the beginning of any cat's life, before the personality, before the opinions, before the knocking of glasses off tables.

A newborn kitten arrives with its eyes sealed shut. They stay that way for roughly the first week to ten days. Hearing is still switching on. The kitten's whole world, in those first days, is built out of three things it can feel without seeing: warmth, vibration, and rhythm.

Warmth from a mother's body and from siblings pressed against each other in a pile. Vibration from the purr, which a mother cat can produce while nursing. And rhythm, the steady pulse of a living body that is right there, every second, for as long as the kitten needs it.

That's the first environment. Not a room. Not a toy. A pile of bodies with a heartbeat in it.

Then something happens that every cat owner has seen and few have thought hard about. A fully grown cat, sleek and independent and entirely too proud to admit it needs anything, climbs onto a soft blanket and starts to knead. Slow, rhythmic, paws pressing in and out. Eyes half closed. Sometimes a faint purr.

The popular explanation, and a sensible one, is that kneading is a leftover from nursing, when kittens press on the mother to bring the milk down. The adult cat isn't hungry. The adult cat is remembering how safe felt.

Which raises a question I can't stop turning over.

If a cat's earliest memory of safety has a pulse in it, what happens when an adult cat is alone in a quiet house for nine hours?

We like to say cats are fine on their own. Many are. Cats are crepuscular, they sleep somewhere between twelve and sixteen hours a day, and a well-adjusted cat can pass a quiet afternoon with the calm of a monk.

But "fine" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

Plenty of cats, especially indoor ones, live in a world that is almost entirely silent for a large part of the day. The refrigerator hums. The radiator ticks. A car passes. And then, around the time the key turns in the lock, the whole apartment comes alive again.

Humans are very good at reading the way dogs feel about being left. The whining, the pacing, the shredded cushions. Cats are far better at hiding it. A cat that is struggling with solitude rarely does anything dramatic. It sleeps in odd places. It overgrooms. It waits at the door a little too long. It becomes very, very attached to the one warm thing in the house that doesn't leave.

If you've ever had a cat that follows you from room to room, that sleeps pressed against your ribs, that settles only when it can feel you breathing, you already know what I'm describing.

They aren't looking for a toy.

They're looking for a pulse.

And that is the idea that someone, somewhere, decided to build a product around.

Let's talk about what a heartbeat actually is to a mammal, because it's more interesting than it sounds.

A heartbeat is the first sound most mammals ever experience. Before light, before language, before any voice, there is a rhythm. In humans, a developing baby spends months inside a body that is thumping away at a steady pace, and the old folk wisdom that newborns settle when held against a chest is almost universal. Parents have known it for as long as there have been parents.

Animal keepers know a version of it too. For generations, people raising a lonely puppy or kitten have tucked a ticking clock or a warm bottle into the bedding on the first night home. Some swear by it. Others roll their eyes. The honest truth is that the scientific evidence for the ticking-clock trick is thin, and anyone who tells you it is a proven cure for a homesick animal is selling something.

But the intuition behind it is hard to dismiss. A slow, steady rhythm, paired with warmth and a soft body, is the closest thing a young animal gets to a signal that says: you are not alone.

Now add one more fact. A cat's own heart is not like ours. A resting adult cat's heart typically beats somewhere around 140 to 220 times a minute, depending on the cat, the moment, and how relaxed it is. Ours sits at roughly 60 to 100. A cat's whole life runs on a faster clock.

That means a convincing heartbeat for a cat is not a human heartbeat. It's a different tempo, a different weight, a different feel.

Which makes the idea at the center of this post either very clever or completely absurd.

And the only creature qualified to judge is the one with the whiskers.

Here is what nobody tells you about cats and fakes.

A cat is a precision instrument. Its nose can pick up scent information we cannot imagine. Its whiskers read air movement and tiny changes in space. Its hearing reaches far above the range of human ears, high enough to catch the squeak of a mouse a room away. Its eyes are built for dim light. This is an animal engineered over millions of years to detect the difference between something alive and something that only looks alive.

Which is why most "realistic" cat toys fail so fast. The fur is right. The shape is right. And the cat knows in about a second and a half that nothing inside is moving.

Cats have been living near humans for something like ten thousand years. Archaeologists found a cat buried alongside a person on Cyprus roughly 9,500 years ago, which tells us the bond is ancient. But even after all that time sharing hearths and barns and sofas, cats never lost their instinct for spotting a bluff.

That's what makes any object that claims to comfort a cat such a risky claim. You cannot persuade a cat with a label. You cannot reason with it. You cannot post a five-star review that it will read.

The cat decides in its own time, on its own terms, with its own body.

It will either walk past, or it will do something else.

I won't tell you which. That part belongs to the cat.

There's a reason this kind of object lands so hard with people, and it has nothing to do with plush.

Gifts for pets are never really for pets. They're for the part of us that feels guilty at 7:40 in the morning when the door closes and a small face watches us leave. They're for the version of us that wishes we could be two places at once. They're for the quiet apology that no cat will ever accept and no cat will ever need.

That's not cynical. That's love, working with the tools it has.

And the strangest thing about caring for an animal is how much of the work is guesswork. The cat can't tell you what it needs. It can't say "I'm lonely" or "I'm anxious about the new furniture" or "that vacuum cleaner is a personal enemy." You get signals. A slow blink. A tail held high. Ears turned flat. A cat that curls up in the exact spot where your jumper was.

Researchers at the University of Sussex reported in 2020 that cats were more likely to approach a person who slow-blinked at them, which suggests even the smallest gestures, well timed, carry meaning in the cat's world.

Small gestures. Large effects.

That might be the single most useful thing a cat owner can learn. You don't need a grand gesture. You need the right small one, delivered at the right moment, in the language the animal actually speaks.

Warmth is a language. Rhythm is a language. Closeness is a language.

The only question is whether a person can learn to speak it through an object.

Now the season matters, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't.

Winter changes a household. The nights come early. The heating goes on. People stay in, and then they don't. They go away for the holidays, or they fill the house with guests, or they drag a tree through the front door and cover it in lights. To a cat, a living room that was a predictable kingdom in October becomes a place where the furniture moves, strangers appear, and strange smells arrive in bags.

Many cats handle all of it beautifully. Some hide under the bed until January.

Most owners I know have a version of the same Christmas story. The cat who ignored every wrapped present and fell asleep inside the wrapping paper. The cat who treated the tree as a personal jungle gym. The cat who, after the guests had gone, went straight to the one soft thing in the room and refused to move.

That last cat is the one I think about.

Because after the noise ends, what does a cat reach for? Not the toys. Not the treats. It reaches for whatever feels like the end of the day. Something warm. Something that holds still. Something that, to a very small and very sensitive animal, feels like it is breathing.

A gift that understands that is a different category of gift.

It isn't there to entertain. It's there to stay.

I should be straight with you, because trust is the only currency that matters when a post gets this long.

A plush with a mechanism inside it is not a cure. It's not a vet. It's not a substitute for your time, your attention, or a proper bed and a proper diet and a house a cat feels safe in. If a cat is truly distressed when left alone, if it stops eating, cries for hours, overgrooms to the point of bald patches, soils outside the litter tray, that deserves a conversation with a veterinarian, not a shopping cart.

And the claim in the video, that the heartbeat calms and comforts, is exactly that: a claim. A promise made by a caption. Cats are individuals. Some fall in love with a thing in a day. Some never notice it. Some sniff it once, file it under "unimportant," and go back to staring at a wall.

That's not a flaw in the idea. It's the honest nature of cats.

But here's why I keep coming back to it anyway.

Almost every cat product on the market is designed to make a human feel something. This one is built around a question the cat might actually care about. Not "what will she find fun?" but "what does she find safe?"

That's a better question. Even if the answer turns out to be different for every cat in your life.

And there's only one way to see how a cat answers it.

Maybe the deeper issue is that we've misread cats for centuries.

The stereotype is that cats are aloof. Independent. Barely interested in us beyond the can opener. It's a flattering story for people who prefer their pets low-maintenance, and it has quietly shaped how the whole pet industry treats them.

Then researchers started testing it.

In 2019, a team led by Kristyn Vitale at Oregon State University published a study in Current Biology adapting a classic attachment test, the kind used on human infants and dogs, for cats. Roughly two-thirds of the cats showed a secure attachment to their owners, a share in the same range as infants. The cats took comfort from their person's return and used them as a base from which to explore.

Read that against the stereotype. The aloof cat is, for most cats, a story we told ourselves.

What looks like indifference is often a quieter dialect. Cats don't stand at the window howling. They don't throw their whole bodies at you in the doorway. They sit nearby. They check. They keep you in their peripheral awareness the way a tide keeps the shore.

If that's true, then a lot of cat behavior reads differently. The cat that appears at the bathroom door. The cat that sleeps on your side of the bed the moment you leave it. The cat that chooses to be in the room, but not on you, close enough to hear you breathe.

That's attachment. It simply doesn't make a lot of noise.

And attachment, unlike entertainment, is something you can feel at three in the morning.

Which brings us, finally, to the box.

In 2014, researchers at Utrecht University in the Netherlands studied newly arrived cats in an animal shelter. Some were given a simple cardboard hiding box. Others were not. The cats with boxes settled in faster and showed lower stress scores in the first days.

So the box doesn't win because cats are unreasonable. The box wins because it solves a real problem: it makes a small animal feel contained, hidden, and held.

Read that again. Contained. Hidden. Held.

Cats don't look for novelty when they're uneasy. They look for enclosure. They squeeze into drawers, shopping bags, laundry baskets, the gap behind the sofa, a sink you were about to use. They find the tightest, warmest, quietest space in the house and make it theirs.

And now you can see why the pet aisle keeps failing. It sells things to look at. The cat is looking for something to lean on.

Every cat owner has watched this happen in miniature. The cat who ignores the expensive bed and sleeps in the laundry you just folded. The cat who chooses the lap of the one person in the room who dislikes cats. The cat who ends up pressed into the warm hollow you left in the duvet.

Comfort, for a cat, is not decoration. It's contact.

So any object that wants to earn a place in a cat's life has to pass a very old test. Not "is it interesting?"

Is it safe enough to sleep against?

There's one more piece of cat biology that quietly rewires how you think about all this.

Purring.

Most people assume a purr means a cat is happy, and often it does. But cats also purr when they're hurt, when they're frightened, when they're giving birth, and when they're being examined at the vet. Researchers have long noted that the purr falls into a low-frequency range, commonly cited as somewhere between about 25 and 150 hertz, and some scientists have speculated that it may help a cat soothe itself. That part is still debated, and you should be wary of anyone who treats it as settled.

What isn't debated is the pattern. A purr is a rhythm. A low, steady, repeating vibration, produced by the cat, felt through its own body, shared with whatever is pressed against it.

A cat that purrs against you is broadcasting something. A cat that purrs alone is talking to itself.

Think about what that implies. A cat's most reliable comfort signal is rhythmic, bodily, and close. It's a sound you feel as much as hear.

So the idea that a cat might respond to a steady pulse, low and warm, held right against its chest, isn't an absurd leap. It's an extension of the way the animal already soothes itself.

Whether it works for your cat is a separate question. But the question is a good one.

And good questions are what make people hit play.

I've watched a lot of animal content. Rescues, reunions, strange friendships, birds adopting kittens, dogs guarding sleeping babies. After a while you develop a feel for what actually works on the human nervous system, and it's rarely the thing the creator thinks it is.

It isn't the spectacle. It's the decision.

A person can watch a thousand clips of cats doing cat things and feel nothing. But put a cat in front of something unfamiliar and let it decide, and a room full of strangers leans in. Because the cat's reaction can't be faked, can't be directed, can't be hurried. It happens in the animal's own timing.

There's a small, old thrill in watching a creature choose.

We live in a world of curated reactions. Influencers perform surprise. Brands rehearse authenticity. A cat will do none of it. A cat will not act pleased for the camera. If it hates the thing, you will know in one second. If it loves the thing, you will know that too, and it will feel earned, because you watched the cat make up its mind.

That's why fifteen seconds is plenty.

Fifteen seconds is enough time for a cat to walk across a room, make a judgment, and change the way you think about a very small object.

I'm not going to tell you what the cat decides.

I'll just say that I've seen a lot of reactions in my time, and I did not see this one coming.

Let me ask you something that has nothing to do with a plush.

Who in your life is waiting for a pulse?

Not literally. I mean the cat who sleeps at the door at 4 p.m. and doesn't know why. The older cat who moves more slowly this year and has started choosing the radiator over the windowsill. The shy rescue who has lived with you for months and still keeps one eye open while sleeping. The new arrival who cried the first three nights in a strange house. The one who wakes at 3 a.m. and walks the length of the hallway, looking for something she can't name.

Every cat has a version of that. Most of us call it personality.

Sometimes it's personality. Sometimes it's an animal doing the best it can with a nervous system built for a much busier, more crowded, more physically close world than the one we've given it.

The idea behind this particular gift is almost embarrassingly simple. It doesn't try to entertain. It doesn't promise to fix. It offers a soft body, a steady rhythm, and a place to put a chin.

And honestly, that may be the most cat-aware thing a person can give a cat.

Not a thing to chase.

A thing to rest against.

The best gifts you've ever received probably weren't expensive.

They were accurate.

Somebody noticed something about you that you hadn't said out loud. The book that arrived a week after the bad week. The scarf in exactly your color. The tiny, odd thing that proved they had been listening when you thought nobody was.

That's what accuracy feels like. It's the opposite of generic.

A cat can't write a wishlist, so the burden of accuracy falls entirely on the person. You have to watch. You have to learn which corner of the house she keeps returning to, which fabric she kneads, what time of day she gets restless, how she behaves when the front door closes behind you. You have to interpret a creature who speaks in posture and silence.

Which means the real gift, the one underneath all the other gifts, is attention.

An object can only be as good as the attention that chose it. A plush chosen because it was cute is a plush. A plush chosen because you noticed your cat gravitates toward warm, soft, steady things is an answer to a question you asked by paying attention.

That difference never shows up on a product page. But it shows up in the house. In whether the thing gets used or gets ignored. In whether the cat treats it as furniture or as company.

So if there's a lesson hiding in a fifteen-second clip about a stuffed animal, maybe it's this.

Don't shop for the cat you imagine.

Shop for the cat who actually lives with you.

I know exactly what the comment section is going to say, because I've read this comment section before.

"My cat would destroy it in four minutes."

Fair. Some cats are hunters first and snugglers second. A cat that wrestles everything it meets might treat a soft toy as prey, and that's worth knowing before you buy anything. Watch how your cat treats stuffed objects. If she kicks, bites, and disembowels them, a heartbeat won't change her personality.

"My cat doesn't care about toys."

Also fair. Some cats genuinely don't. Some will sniff an object once and walk off for good. Cats are not an audience you can win by volume.

"This is a gimmick."

Maybe. Plenty of pet products are. A healthy amount of skepticism is exactly right, especially when a caption makes a promise about calming an animal. If you do look into one, treat it like any pet purchase. Read independent reviews, check that anything with a battery or electronics is securely enclosed, make sure no small parts can come loose, and keep an eye on how your cat uses it, particularly in the first days. If she chews it open, it goes away.

None of that makes the question less interesting.

It makes it more honest. The people who will love this idea are not the people who believe in magic. They're the people who have watched a cat curl against a warm laundry basket and thought, there must be something more deliberate than that.

And the people who are skeptical?

Good. You're the audience this was made for. Cats are skeptics too.

If you take only one practical thing from this post, let it be this.

A cat's sense of safety is built from many small ingredients, and an object is only one of them. Before anything arrives in a box, it's worth asking whether the basics are in place.

Does she have somewhere to hide that no one will disturb? Cats like options at different heights, so a shelf, a cat tree, or the top of a bookcase can matter as much as a bed. Is there a predictable routine? Cats read time through habit, and meals, play, and quiet hours that arrive at the same moments tell an animal that the world is stable. Does the house have enough of her scent in it? A blanket she sleeps on, unwashed for a few days, can do more than a new purchase. Is there a calm place away from the loud parts of the household when guests arrive?

And is there play, real play, with you, for a few minutes each day? A cat that gets to stalk, pounce, and catch sleeps differently afterward.

Get those right, and a soft companion becomes an extra, not a crutch. Get them wrong, and no object, no matter how clever, will rescue a cat who feels unsafe in her own house.

That's the part that gets forgotten when something goes viral. The thing that gets shared is the object. The thing that works is the home.

I say this because I want you to leave with something better than a product.

I want you to leave looking at your cat differently.

Watch her for ten minutes tonight. See where she sleeps. See what she leans against. See what she chooses when nobody is choosing for her.

That is the real shopping list.

One last thought before the cat gets the final word.

We spend so much energy trying to make animals fit our idea of a good life. Bigger towers. Smarter feeders. Louder toys. Meanwhile the animal on the rug is asking for something so old it predates every product ever sold: to be near something warm that is quietly alive.

If an object can honor that, even a little, even for one cat, it deserves a look. Not because it is magic, but because it listens to what the cat has been saying all along, in the only language she has, and that's closeness.

So here is where I'll leave it.

A white cat. A soft object. A very old rhythm. And a caption that dares to claim the perfect gift for cats does exist after all.

I don't know if it's true for every cat. I'd be lying if I said I did. What I know is that I've spent years watching people try to buy affection from animals that can't be bought, and I've never seen a fifteen-second clip make me rethink the entire approach so quickly.

Because it flips the question. It stops asking what a cat might find amusing and starts asking what a cat might find like home.

That's a different kind of gift. A quieter one.

And it has a way of making you wonder who else in your house, or in your life, has been waiting for something steady to rest against, and never found a way to ask.

Watch the video. Look at the cat, not the object. Notice the moment her attention changes. Then ask yourself the question I couldn't stop asking.

Who needs one?

text:
🗞️18 November 2026 | Daily Edition: Pre-Market

Nvidia Lifted Futures, Bitcoin Stopped Short of the Weekly Close

Nvidia's beat lifted stock futures and pulled Bitcoin to $65,199 after the bell, but IBIT's selling came back, the Binance hackers moved another $142 million of Ether and Europe sold the morning back toward $64,100, with the Fed minutes due at 2:00 PM EST.

Prepared around 5:50 AM EST on Wednesday 18 November. This edition picks up from Tuesday's US Close, prepared at 4:10 PM EST, and only adds what happened since: Nvidia's results, the evening session, Asia and the first hours of Europe. Crypto prices are live prints as of about 5:45 AM EST, and futures, oil, Treasury, dollar and gold figures are live overnight prints.

1⃣ Bitcoin broke Tuesday's ceiling after the bell, then handed most of it back

Bitcoin was near $63,930 at last night's edition. It made its evening low of about $63,870 in the 4:00 PM EST bar, then cleared the $64,050 ceiling that had capped it four times on Tuesday afternoon and reached about $64,600 in the 4:30 PM EST bar. When stock futures reopened at 6:00 PM EST on Nvidia's results, it jumped to $65,199, about $115 short of the $65,315 weekly close. Tuesday's daily candle closed near $64,875 at 7:00 PM EST, just above Monday's $64,815 close. The fade started at 8:00 PM EST and found a floor at about $64,035 to $64,070 in the 9:00 PM EST hour, right on the old ceiling. Asia's best was about $64,890 at 2:45 AM EST. Europe sold from about $64,580 at 5:05 AM EST to a low of about $64,095 at 5:35 AM EST, and Bitcoin trades near $64,250, about 0.5% above last night's edition and roughly flat over 24 hours.

🖊️ Market significance: The breakout through $64,050 held as support twice overnight, but the rally stalled below the weekly close for a fourth time in three days.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Turning yesterday's ceiling into a floor is real progress. Still, the best risk news of the week only bought about 2% from last night's low, and that tells me sellers are still waiting above $65,000.

2⃣ Ether was turned back under $1,835 again, XRP touched $1

Ether rose from about $1,801 at last night's edition to $1,834 in the 6:00 PM EST bar, just under the $1,835 to $1,842 band that has capped it since the weekly close. It held about $1,795 in the 9:00 PM EST hour, reached about $1,818 in Asia at 2:45 AM EST and slipped to about $1,796 at 5:35 AM EST. It trades near $1,802, flat against last night's edition and about 0.5% higher over 24 hours. XRP was the overnight leader: it briefly traded above $1.00 at about 3:15 AM EST and is near $0.997, up about 4% over 24 hours. Solana peaked at $75.70 at 6:00 PM EST and is near $74.65, up about 3% over 24 hours, as its London conference wrapped up. Zcash is near $936 to $939 and HYPE near $68.25 to $68.50.

🖊️ Market significance: Ether has now been turned back at or just under the same band four times since Sunday night, while XRP and Solana carried the relative strength.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Rotation into XRP and Solana while Ether stalls is not a market-wide bid. I need Ether to close above $1,842 before I treat it as anything more than a range.

3⃣ On-chain traders added Bitcoin longs while offshore funding turned negative

Bitcoin open interest on the largest on-chain perps venue rose about 3.1% since last night's edition to about 38,700 BTC, while on a large offshore exchange it was flat at about 31,170 BTC, with price up about 0.5%. Funding split: the on-chain venue pays longs about +0.01% per eight hours, while the offshore exchange is slightly negative at about -0.002%. In Ether, the pattern flipped: open interest fell about 1.5% on the on-chain venue to about 608,300 ETH but rose about 3.4% offshore to about 687,800 ETH, with offshore funding slightly negative. Solana and XRP funding on the on-chain venue is negative despite their gains.

🖊️ Market significance: Overnight positioning was a two-way trade, with on-chain longs chasing the Nvidia bounce while offshore traders kept a small short bias.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Negative funding on Solana and XRP while they rally is the cleanest squeeze setup on the board. In Bitcoin, if the new on-chain longs were added on the jump toward $65,000, they are now under water, and that is fuel for the downside if $64,000 breaks.

4⃣ IBIT's one-day pause ended, Goldman showed a large Ether fund book

Tuesday's spot Bitcoin ETFs lost about $239.9 million, with BlackRock's IBIT down about $209.5 million, Grayscale's GBTC down $17.7 million and ARK's ARKB down $13.1 million, against small inflows into Morgan Stanley's fund and Grayscale's mini trust. Monday's final count had shown IBIT taking in about $76.5 million, its first inflow in more than a week. Spot Ether ETFs lost about $29.1 million, almost all from BlackRock's ETHA, their sixth outflow in seven sessions. Separately, Goldman Sachs' third-quarter 13F shows about $1.22 billion across seven spot Ether ETFs at 30 September, up from about $211.6 million in June, led by about 29.96 million ETHA shares worth about $602.9 million.

🖊️ Market significance: Monday's IBIT inflow did not start a streak. The biggest Bitcoin fund was back to being the main source of selling within a day.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Goldman's Ether book is a 30 September snapshot, taken before Ether's slide into the $1,800s. Today's flows matter more to me: one inflow day followed by a $210 million outflow is still a distribution pattern.

5⃣ DBS opened 24/7 USDC minting for Asian institutions, Tether funded a payments network

Singapore's DBS, Southeast Asia's largest bank, said eligible institutional clients in Asia can now mint and redeem USDC directly through the bank, with dollar and stablecoin settlement around the clock, building on its work with Circle in the Monetary Authority of Singapore's Project BLOOM. Separately, Tether's investment arm took a strategic stake in Stables, which connects local banking systems to USDT settlement across more than 160 markets and handles more than $2 billion of annual USDT volume. Early this morning, about 250 million USDC was minted at the issuer's treasury. USDT supply is about $175.2 billion to $175.3 billion and USDC about $68.9 billion to $69.2 billion.

🖊️ Market significance: The region's biggest bank becoming a direct USDC on-ramp removes a reliance on exchange liquidity for institutions that want stablecoins outside banking hours.

🗨️ My viewpoint: After the World Bank news on Tuesday, this is the second large institutional USDC channel in two days. Supply has not turned up yet, but a fresh 250 million mint is the kind of sign I watch for.

6⃣ Tokenized Anthropic exposure sold out at $500 million, Maple wants to lend against tokenized stocks

A Binance Wallet campaign selling tokenized exposure to Anthropic's IPO filled its 500 million USDC cap on Wednesday, inside an eight-hour window that opened at 1:00 AM EST. The tokens, called ANTx and issued by Backed through xStocks, were offered at an indicative 70 to 78 USDC each with a 5% fee. They track the price only, carry no voting or dividend rights, and can be backed by cash rather than shares. Separately, Maple Finance chief executive Sidney Powell said he targets $10 billion to $15 billion in assets by the end of 2027, from $4.7 billion at the end of the third quarter, and expects tokenized stocks to grow five to tenfold next year, allowing Maple to lend against tokenized shares. Maple is also in talks with banks about funding its Bitcoin-backed loans.

🖊️ Market significance: Half a billion dollars of stablecoins went into synthetic pre-IPO exposure in hours, while Bitcoin ETFs lost $240 million.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is the competition for crypto's marginal dollar in one number. Stablecoin holders are not leaving crypto rails, they are buying AI exposure on them, and that keeps the bid away from Bitcoin.

7⃣ The Binance hackers moved another 78,415 ETH

Wallets tied to the 29 October Binance theft moved about 78,415 ETH, roughly $142 million, overnight, split across six new addresses of 12,000 ETH each and one of 6,415 ETH, and continued swapping the Ether into Bitcoin through THORChain, according to on-chain trackers. Five of the 12,000 ETH transfers landed within about four minutes, from 2:48 AM EST. Together with Tuesday morning's 74,880 ETH, that is more than 153,000 ETH, about $280 million, moved in about a day, from a pile of more than 600,000 ETH held before Tuesday.

🖊️ Market significance: A second batch of about $140 million followed the first within a day, so the laundering is now steady rather than occasional.

🗨️ My viewpoint: These swaps go through cross-chain routers, not exchange order books, so the direct price impact is limited. But every batch adds Ether supply into thin overnight hours, and the 2:48 AM EST batch landed just after Ether's Asia high.

8⃣ Ledger implants reached Dubai, Etherscan flagged an access attempt

Two Ledger owners reported losing about $604,000 in total from hardware wallets they said were bought at Virgin Megastore in Dubai, a Ledger-authorised retailer: about 1,300 SOL from a Ledger Flex, which an independent implant registry confirmed as containing a hidden hardware implant, and 507,000 USDT from a Ledger Stax, where an implant is suspected. Separately, Etherscan said it detected unauthorized attempts to access its customer support ticketing system, has put preventive measures in place, has not confirmed any data exposure and warned users about impersonators.

🖊️ Market significance: Supply-chain attacks on hardware wallets have now spread beyond resellers in Asia and Europe to an authorised retailer in the Gulf.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Self-custody depends on trusting the device, and that trust now depends on where it was bought. For anyone holding size, I would treat any device bought through a reseller as suspect until it is checked.

9⃣ Coinbase's AI agent stopped a deepfake scam, a Scattered Spider hacker got six years

Coinbase said its AI scam defences stopped about $4.7 million from leaving customer accounts during a fake Tesla crypto giveaway that used a deepfake of Elon Musk, blocking about 91% of the attempted transfers with no human in the loop. More than 500,000 people watched the fake livestream. Separately, Scottish hacker Tyler Buchanan, linked by prosecutors to the Scattered Spider group, was sentenced in California to six years in federal prison over a phishing and SIM-swap scheme that stole at least $11.6 million in crypto. He is the last of five defendants sentenced.

🖊️ Market significance: AI is now on both sides of crypto fraud, used to fake the pitch and to stop the transfer.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The detail that matters is that nobody was hacked: hundreds of customers chose to send money. Platforms that can stop authorised scam transfers at that rate will have an edge with regulators and with banks.

1⃣0⃣ Bitwise filed for a Zcash ETF on the Texas Stock Exchange

Bitwise filed an S-1 for a spot Zcash ETF late on Tuesday, with shares expected to list on the Texas Stock Exchange under the ticker ZEC, Coinbase Custody as custodian and the fee still left blank. It would compete with Grayscale's Zcash fund, which already trades on NYSE Arca. Zcash is up about 1.5% to 2% over 24 hours.

🖊️ Market significance: This is a second major issuer betting on a privacy coin ETF, and a new exchange competing for crypto listings.

🗨️ My viewpoint: An S-1 is a filing, not an approval, and the existing Zcash fund reported no flows on Tuesday. The listing choice matters more to me than the coin: Texas is positioning itself as a home for crypto products.

1⃣1⃣ MEXC's card goes dark today, Hong Kong wants AI agents watching wallets

MEXC said its Global Card will stop working at 10:30 AM EST today, a week after its Asia-Pacific card was discontinued. The exchange blames changes by an unnamed third-party issuer, and it comes after a US Treasury order cutting MEXC off from US financial institutions, which takes effect on 10 December. In Hong Kong, Monetary Authority executive director Raymond Chan said the regulator is exploring AI agents that combine blockchain analytics, customer data and wallet freezing to detect crypto money laundering, citing more than $150 billion received by illicit addresses in 2025, 84% of it in stablecoins.

🖊️ Market significance: Offshore exchanges are losing payment partners ahead of the US order, while Asian regulators move toward automated on-chain monitoring.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Card networks and issuers act before the legal deadline, which is how US financial sanctions really bite. I watch whether other offshore venues lose banking partners before 10 December.

1⃣2⃣ MARA kept moving Bitcoin out after its results

On-chain trackers show MARA moved out about 1,713.9 BTC, about $121 million, in the eight days after its 10 November results, including 366 BTC on Tuesday afternoon, transfers they read as sales, although the receiving wallets are not confirmed as exchanges. MARA's own disclosures show it sold 13,597 BTC between 1 October and 10 November and 40,581 BTC so far in 2026, at an average of about $74,446.

🖊️ Market significance: The largest listed miner has gone from a long-term holder to a steady seller.

🗨️ My viewpoint: About $15 million a day of miner supply is easy to absorb in a normal market. In a week with ETF outflows and laundered Ether, it is one more seller the bid has to take out.

1⃣3⃣ The biggest Ether dip buyers look finished, an XRP whale moved to storage

Wallets linked to Erik Voorhees have now bought 92,052 ETH, about $165.6 million, over the past week at an average of about $1,921, and sit on about $11 million of unrealized losses. A separate tracker says November's largest on-chain dip buyer has spent all of its stablecoins after buying 95,020 ETH in six days at an average of about $1,906, taking its holdings to about 649,650 ETH. In XRP, a holder whose wallets trace back to a 2020 exchange withdrawal moved 281 million XRP, about $270 million, into two wallets over three weeks, the latest batch on Tuesday morning. Both wallets were set up a month earlier with test transfers, a pattern that points to custody rather than a sale.

🖊️ Market significance: The two largest dip buyers in Ether appear to be done buying, so the support they provided below $1,900 is fading.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Both buyers are under water at $1,802. If they stay patient, the supply is locked away. If $1,749 breaks, their losses become a story the market will trade.

1⃣4⃣ Analysts see a bid wall near $60,000 as demand keeps shrinking

An on-chain analytics firm said Bitcoin has returned to a bearish phase, with its analyst sentiment index at its most bearish since November 2025 and total demand growth contracting at its fastest pace since 1 July. It sees support between $62,000 and $65,000 but no confirmed bottom. A second firm's order-book analysis shows resting bids within 5% of price outweighing asks by about 2.3 times on two of the largest spot venues, with the biggest single bid level near $60,000 the largest on one venue since August, and said most forced liquidations have already happened. It also said realized losses have reached levels seen only near the 2018, 2020, 2022 and early 2023 lows.

🖊️ Market significance: Demand data and order books disagree. Flows are weak, but there is a large wall of resting bids below the market.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Resting bids can be pulled, so I treat the $60,000 wall as a magnet as much as a floor. Capitulation-level losses are what bottoms look like, but they do not tell me the timing.

1⃣5⃣ Nvidia beat and raised, Nasdaq futures rose about 1.1%

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, against about $109 billion expected, with adjusted earnings of $2.68 a share against about $2.47 to $2.48. It guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above the roughly $125.1 billion expected, raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to about 75% from 70% and included no China data center compute revenue. The board said it will not reinstate Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares are up about 3% to 4% in premarket trading from Tuesday's $155.46 close. S&P 500 futures are up about 0.6% near 7,401, Nasdaq 100 futures about 1.1% near 27,365 and Dow futures about 0.3% near 50,946. In Asia, Korea's KOSPI rose about 2.0% to 5,067, the Nikkei about 0.3% and the Hang Seng fell about 0.9%. Europe's Stoxx 50 and the DAX are each up about 0.2%.

🖊️ Market significance: The AI trade got the confirmation it needed after Tuesday's 850-point Dow drop, and futures held most of their after-hours gain.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Futures peaked at the 6:00 PM EST reopen, faded into midnight and then recovered, the same path Bitcoin took, except Bitcoin has not recovered. That gap is the clearest sign this week that crypto is not trading the risk-on signal.

1⃣6⃣ Oil fell on a stock build, gold dropped below $3,800, the dollar firmed

Brent crude is near $92, down about 1.2%, and WTI is near $83.20, down about 1.7%, after industry data showed US crude stocks rose by about 5.3 million barrels last week against an expected draw. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5.09% to 5.10%, about 1 basis point lower. The dollar index is up about 0.25% near 103.75, and gold futures are down about 2.4% near $3,772.

🖊️ Market significance: Gold's slide alongside a firmer dollar shows rate-hike expectations, not fear, driving the macro tape this morning.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Gold falling more than 2% on a calm morning tells me higher real rates are pulling money out of non-yielding assets. Bitcoin has not been trading with tech this week, so it gets little help from the Nvidia rally, while the rate pressure hitting gold applies to it as well.

1⃣7⃣ Housing data at 8:30 AM EST, the Fed minutes at 2:00 PM EST

October housing starts and building permits are due at 8:30 AM EST, the weekly government crude inventory report at 10:30 AM EST, a 20-year Treasury bond auction at 1:00 PM EST and remarks from Fed Governor Michael Barr at 1:35 PM EST. The main event is the minutes of the 27 to 28 October Fed meeting at 2:00 PM EST. In crypto, MEXC's card shuts at 10:30 AM EST, and pricing for Anthropic's IPO, which sets the final terms for the tokenized campaign, is expected.

🖊️ Market significance: With the 10-year above 5% and Fed officials split between several hikes and no dramatic action, the minutes are the day's real test.

🗨️ My viewpoint: A 20-year auction an hour before the minutes makes the early afternoon the riskiest window of the day. A weak auction plus hawkish minutes is the combination that could push Bitcoin back through $64,000.

🗨️ My Overall Viewpoint:
The night gave me a better structure but not a better trend. Bitcoin broke through the $64,050 ceiling that capped it all Tuesday afternoon, used Nvidia's beat to reach $65,199, and then defended the old ceiling twice, at about $64,035 in the 9:00 PM EST hour and $64,095 this morning. That is a real improvement. But the rally stopped below the $65,315 weekly close for a fourth time, IBIT went back to selling $210 million a day, the two biggest Ether dip buyers appear to be done, the Binance hackers moved a second $140 million batch of Ether and MARA is still moving coins out. Under the price, the build-out kept going: DBS made USDC a 24/7 bank product in Asia, Tether funded a payments network, Bitwise filed for a Zcash ETF and a $500 million tokenized Anthropic campaign filled in hours, which also shows where speculative money wants to be.

For the US session, my Bitcoin support is $64,035 to $64,095, the overnight lows on Tuesday's old ceiling, then $63,870, last night's post-close low, $63,770, then $63,377 to $63,257, Tuesday's retest and low, and $61,950, Saturday night's low, with the long cluster between $59,500 and $62,200 and the bid wall near $60,000 below it. Resistance is $64,890, the Asia high, then $65,199, the overnight high, and $65,315 to $65,383, the weekly close and Tuesday's high. A daily close above $65,383 would end the run of rejections, while losing $64,000 would put the afternoon lows back in play. For Ether, support is $1,795, the overnight lows, then $1,790, $1,765 and $1,749, Tuesday's low. Resistance is $1,818, the Asia high, then $1,834, the overnight high, and the $1,835 to $1,842 band. I stay defensive but less so than last night. I watch the 8:30 AM EST housing data, the 1:00 PM EST bond auction, the 2:00 PM EST Fed minutes and Wednesday's ETF flows tonight. These are my analytical levels, not forecasts, and nothing here is financial advice.

Is another US-Iran war looming?
Washington has deployed a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as peace talks stall and hostilities with Tehran intensify
Published 18 Nov, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/9EiLjGtOad
The US has deployed a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as tensions with Iran flare again, raising fears of another round of large-scale fighting.
Nearly nine months after the US-Israeli bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic began, international efforts to end the conflict remain stalled. President Donald Trump has threatened further strikes while insisting that the war is effectively over.
How big is the US military buildup?
US Central Command announced on Monday that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had arrived in the Middle East after departing San Diego in September, bringing thousands of additional personnel to the region.
The Roosevelt and its accompanying strike group join the USS George H.W. Bush, which arrived in April, and the USS George Washington, deployed in August. The Pentagon last had three carrier strike groups in the region simultaneously in April, for the first time since 2003.
According to the US Navy, the American fleet in the Arabian Sea also includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, with two additional destroyers stationed in the Red Sea. An accompanying amphibious group carrying around 2,000 Marines aboard three ships has yet to arrive.
The Roosevelt was initially expected to relieve the George Washington, although it remains unclear how long all three carriers will operate in the region simultaneously.
What’s behind the latest escalation?
The IRGC has launched several drone attacks against American facilities, accusing Washington of hostile military operations and violations of Iranian airspace.
US military installations in Bahrain came under attack three times in five days, most recently on Tuesday, when Iranian drones targeted a radar installation at Sheikh Isa Air Base.
Washington responded hours later with what it described as a “self-defense” strike against an IRGC missile launch site on Iran’s Qeshm Island, near the entrance to the Persian Gulf.
What happened to the ceasefire?
The US-Israeli strikes on Iran, launched on February 28, prompted retaliatory attacks by Tehran against American military bases and other US- and Israeli-linked targets across the Middle East. Iran effectively closed the vital Strait of Hormuz, while Washington imposed its own blockade of Iranian ports.
The two sides agreed to a ceasefire in April, but subsequent negotiations failed to produce a lasting settlement. A memorandum of understanding signed in June temporarily eased shipping restrictions and allowed 60 days for further talks before mutual accusations of violations derailed the agreement.
Washington reinforced its naval blockade in July and has since announced plans to disrupt land-based supply routes to Iran. Limited exchanges of strikes have continued, fueling fears of a major escalation following the US midterm elections earlier this month.
Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack?
A CNN report on Monday, citing anonymous sources, claimed that Iranian officials had considered a possible chemical or radioactive “dirty bomb” attack in Washington. No officials went on record to confirm a new or credible threat.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the allegations as “rubbish” and accused pro-Israeli media of spreading “Iraq War-style propaganda” about nonexistent weapons of mass destruction to justify renewed hostilities.
Trump said Washington was taking the report seriously and threatened unprecedented consequences. He also warned that American forces were “locked and loaded” and threatened further action over Tehran’s nuclear activities, including at the underground Pickaxe Mountain facility.
Who controls the Strait of Hormuz?
The vital shipping route remains a major flashpoint, with Washington and Tehran both claiming control and issuing conflicting demands to commercial vessels.
Washington says it has cleared the waterway of mines and offers escorts to some ships. However, it continues to intercept and disable vessels traveling to or from Iranian ports, while heavily penalizing shipping companies that pay Tehran’s transit fees.
Iran requires commercial vessels to register with its Persian Gulf Strait Authority, pay transit fees and follow northern routes near Iranian waters. The IRGC has warned ships against using what it calls “unsafe” American-backed routes.
At least six commercial tankers have been struck and damaged by unidentified projectiles this month alone. Iranian officials have attributed such incidents to “disobedient” vessels hitting sea mines after entering restricted waters without permission.
Before the war, roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait. Traffic has since fallen to less than a third of prewar levels, according to maritime intelligence firm Lloyd’s List.
What’s blocking a peace deal?
Washington and Tehran remain divided over the conditions for ending hostilities.
Iran has proposed reopening Hormuz in exchange for the lifting of American sanctions, the release of frozen assets and an end to the blockade. It has also demanded an end to fighting on all fronts, including Israeli operations in Gaza and southern Lebanon.
Washington insists that any agreement must address Iran’s nuclear program. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed Tehran’s conditions as “absurd,” while Trump recently declared that the US no longer needs a deal.
“The ball is now in the American court,” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said last week.
Qatar has led efforts to revive negotiations, supported by Oman and other regional mediators. Although the latest proposals have failed to produce a breakthrough, diplomatic contacts continue.
Has the war hurt Trump politically?
The prolonged conflict has become a political liability for Trump following heavy Republican losses in the November 3 midterms, which cost the party control of both chambers of Congress.
Opposition to the war and its economic consequences, particularly higher fuel and living costs, contributed to voter dissatisfaction, according to exit polls.
Vice President J.D. Vance initially blamed the election setback directly on the Iran war but subsequently rejected suggestions of a split with Trump, insisting that the campaign would not become an open-ended military commitment.
“We’re not going to stay there forever,” he told Fox News on Monday.
Will Trump strike Iran again?
Despite the growing American military presence and sporadic exchanges of fire, Washington appears to favor continued economic and military pressure over another major bombing campaign, according to media reports.
Rubio has argued that mounting “economic pain” will eventually force Tehran to make concessions, as “eventually you have to eat.” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei has accused Washington of committing war crimes through its blockade and sanctions, which deprive civilians of essential supplies.
Gulf countries have urged the White House to avoid renewed strikes, warning of Iranian retaliation against regional energy infrastructure. Former US diplomat Alan Eyre, who worked on nuclear negotiations with Iran, told Reuters that prolonged restrictions on Iranian oil exports could eventually force Tehran to escalate.
Meanwhile, Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pressed Washington to resume military strikes against Iran, reportedly engaging in a heated “shouting match” with Trump during a recent phone call.

text:
US gives Hungary green light to keep buying Russian energy
Washington has renewed Budapest’s sanctions waiver after Prime Minister Peter Magyar urged Trump to keep Russian supplies flowing
Published 18 Nov, 2026(FULL)
https://t.co/8ifkOIys3D
The US has extended Hungary’s exemption from sanctions targeting Russian energy, allowing Budapest to continue buying oil and gas from Moscow, the Hungarian Foreign Ministry has announced. Hungary’s new government sought to renew the waiver in September, despite pledging to reduce its dependence on Russian energy.
The US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has allowed Hungarian energy company MOL to continue buying Russian oil until March 19, 2027, the ministry announced on Tuesday. The previous exemption was due to expire on November 21.
The decision covers transactions involving Russian oil company Lukoil and its trading subsidiary Litasco, allowing MOL to buy crude on the spot market through the Druzhba pipeline and fulfill existing contracts.
OFAC also extended its guidance for Hungarian energy company MVM, covering financial transactions linked to Russian gas transported through the TurkStream pipeline. The ministry said the authorizations could be renewed again.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar had urged Washington to prolong the waiver after US President Donald Trump reached a deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on diesel exports.
“If the US president has concluded an agreement on diesel exports, it would be illogical not to grant Hungary this exemption for at least another year,” Magyar told outlet 444 in October.
Trump lifted restrictions on Russian diesel exports in October to curb rising fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. The move sparked outrage in Kiev and among Washington’s European allies, while a bipartisan group of US senators accused Trump of betraying Ukraine.
The original exemption was secured in November 2025 by Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orban, a vocal critic of Western sanctions on Moscow over the Ukraine conflict.
Washington also granted Slovakia a 120-day extension of its sanctions exemption on Tuesday, according to the country’s Economy Ministry.
Magyar’s government, which took office in April, has pledged to end Hungary’s dependence on Russian energy by 2035 but acknowledges that an immediate cutoff is unrealistic. Moscow supplied around 90% of the country’s crude oil in 2025, according to S&P Global.
The EU remains divided over Russian energy. Brussels has pushed for a complete phaseout by late 2027 while Hungary and Slovakia remain dependent on pipeline supplies.
Despite efforts to cut imports, the bloc bought 36 billion cubic meters of Russian gas in 2025. Russia’s share of EU gas imports fell from 45% in 2021 to 12% in 2025, but the bloc still spent an estimated €7.2 billion on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) last year, nearly €1 billion more than in 2024.

text:
🚨 BREAKING: Mary Peltola has unseated Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, and she won outright. No ranked-choice rounds were needed.

The Associated Press posted its call at 12:33 PM JST Wednesday (10:33 PM ET / 6:33 PM AKST Tuesday). It was the last Senate race of 2026, and it puts the next Senate at 56-44 for Democrats. Peltola, who is Yup'ik, will be Alaska's first Alaska Native senator (Fox News) and its first Democratic senator since Mark Begich, who lost to Sullivan in 2014. She and Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan (Ojibwe) will be the only Native women ever elected to the Senate (Washington Post). Trump carried Alaska by about 13 points in 2024.

📊 The numbers (Alaska Division of Elections, unofficial, 401 of 401 precincts, as of 11:46 AM JST Wed / 5:46 PM AKST Tue)
• Peltola (D) 144,302 (50.12%)
• Sullivan (R, incumbent) 131,844 (45.80%)
• Gerald Heikes (R) 6,105 (2.12%)
• Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. (no party) 4,760 (1.65%)
• Write-ins 885 (0.31%)
• Margin: 12,458 votes. Peltola has more votes than all the other candidates and write-ins combined (143,594)
• Ballots cast: 290,003 of 605,433 registered voters, or 47.9%
• Ranked choice: Alaska only runs elimination rounds when no one tops 50% of first choices. Peltola did, so there were no rounds (NBC, Alaska Beacon)
• Senate: Republicans held 53-47 going in. Democrats flipped 9 seats, the most since 1958 (AP), for 56-44. That 56 is 54 Democrats plus independents Angus King and Bernie Sanders, who caucus with them (NBC). Every Senate race is now called
• Money: more than $100 million spent for and against the two campaigns, the most in state history (Alaska Beacon). Peltola raised $37M directly vs Sullivan's $14M through mid-October (NBC)

🗣️ What people are saying
• Sullivan hasn't conceded. His spokesman Nate Adams said Monday: "Alaskans deserve a complete and accurate count, and we will let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified." The campaign says it will have more to say by the end of the week. As of 8:15 p.m. JST Wednesday (2:15 a.m. AKST), there was no new statement and no updated official count
• Republicans focus on the "Decoy Dan" fight. A New York Times report said Peltola aides and national Democrats helped recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to split the senator's vote. Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted, Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation, and the NRSC asked the FEC to investigate. The DOJ's suit to block certification was dismissed, and the department has appealed
• Critics of ranked choice call it confusing and messy. But voters rejected a repeal for the second time on Nov 3, 53.81% to 46.19% (Alaska Division of Elections, unofficial), after a 2024 repeal failed by about 700 votes (ADN)
• Peltola: "The status quo in D.C. is not working for Alaska." She denies any role in the other Sullivan's candidacy: "I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent"
• Chuck Schumer: "With 56 seats, Democrats are in a prime position to create a durable majority..."
• Analysts: NBC calls it the largest Senate majority either party has held in 16 years. Peltola tied Sullivan to Trump and hit him on inflation and diesel and fuel costs (NBC)

✅ The facts
• AP call: https://t.co/4AO6RtPVmt
• AP story: https://t.co/61KSaLTHM2
• Official results: https://t.co/zsU5S9Pdha
• NBC on the 56-44 math: https://t.co/6HcHsHEP9j
• Alaska Beacon: https://t.co/mZF5QvUEeW
• Repeal vote (ADN, earlier count): https://t.co/JUuM8vKVMV

❓ Unverified or misleading
• ❌ "The decoy cost Sullivan the race": the math doesn't support it. Even if every vote for Heikes and for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had gone to the senator, he'd have 142,709, short of Peltola's 144,302
• ❌ "Dan Sullivan WON, BY A LOT!" (Trump, Truth Social, 4:55 a.m. JST Sunday Nov 8 / 2:55 p.m. ET Saturday Nov 7): no outlet had called the race, and the unofficial count went the other way
• ❓ Whether Peltola's campaign recruited the second Sullivan: alleged, not proven. The Times report rests partly on her fired campaign manager, who later tried to take back her statements. The FBI and state investigations are open, and no one has been charged
• "56-44" is correct only if you count King and Sanders with the Democrats, which is how AP, NBC, Fox, CBS and Reuters all count it

🤔 Nuance
These numbers are unofficial and preliminary. A final ballot count is scheduled for Wednesday in Alaska (Thursday JST), and the state plans to certify on Nov 25. A drop just under 50% would force ranked-choice rounds, but Peltola leads every other candidate combined, so the outcome wouldn't change. The DOJ appeal and the criminal probe are still pending. Our Nov 12 post said at least 55-44 with Alaska undecided. Alaska makes it 56-44.

Was this a referendum on costs, or a backlash to the "Decoy Dan" fight?

Somalia Welcomes US Resumption of Funding for AU Mission Against Al-Shabaab

MOGADISHU (Somali Report) — Somalia on Monday welcomed a decision by the United States to renew support for international military operations against Al-Shabaab, reversing an earlier funding freeze that had threatened the future of the African Union-led mission.

The US State Department announced Sunday that Washington would support a one-year renewal of the mandates of the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) and the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM).

The decision marks a shift in US policy after Washington suspended funding for UNSOS in July, citing frustration with the Somali government's failure to make sufficient progress against Al-Shabaab, take greater responsibility for national security and implement meaningful security sector reforms.

UNSOS provides logistical support, including supplies and operational assistance, to African Union forces deployed in Somalia. Its withdrawal would have severely undermined the ability of AUSSOM troops to sustain military operations against the insurgents.

In a statement, the Somali government thanked what it described as its "steadfast partner", saying the renewed funding reaffirmed the longstanding partnership between Mogadishu and Washington in the fight against terrorism.

The government also said Somali forces were gradually assuming responsibility for military operations previously conducted by international troops, adding that most major cities and large parts of the country were enjoying greater peace and stability.

However, the decision comes amid mounting security and political challenges that have raised questions about the sustainability of Somalia's campaign against Al-Shabaab.

A foreign diplomatic source familiar with Somalia told AFP that the return of American support was welcome but criticised the abrupt changes in Washington's policy, describing them as "madness".

The source, who requested anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly, also questioned why Washington had not used the funding decision to exert pressure on the Somali government over its domestic political disputes.

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has faced growing opposition after constitutional amendments passed in March extended his term by one year, triggering a political dispute and violent clashes with opposition groups.

Last week, Mohamud dismissed the Supreme Court chief justice as the court was preparing to rule on a case challenging the extension of presidential and parliamentary terms.

The security situation has also deteriorated in several areas. Al-Shabaab claimed last month that it had killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an ambush, potentially one of its deadliest attacks in recent years. The government has not published an official death toll.

Uganda, which contributes the largest number of troops to AUSSOM, also announced last month that it planned to withdraw all its forces by the end of 2027, raising further concerns about the mission's future.

The Al-Qaeda-linked group has fought the Somali government for nearly two decades and continues to control significant rural areas in central Somalia. It also maintains extensive financial and business networks across the country, including in Mogadishu.

Somali forces made territorial gains against the militants after Mohamud returned to power in 2022, but much of that progress was reversed by subsequent insurgent counteroffensives.

Washington said the renewed support for UNSOS was intended to contain security threats emanating from Somalia and prevent a wider regional crisis that could undermine American interests.

A diplomatic source told AFP that an internal US assessment had raised concerns that Somalia could slide towards state failure, prompting a reassessment of the funding suspension.

The State Department, however, cautioned that the decision did not represent an indefinite commitment, urging Somalia and the African Union to develop more sustainable regional security arrangements.

Why Florida Small Town Storytelling Feels Like Home

A Florida town can keep a secret longer than a pelican can keep its eye on a fish sandwich. Behind the pastel storefronts, porch swings, and sun-faded historic markers, everybody knows somebody - and somebody always notices when a familiar car is parked where it should not be. That is the particular pleasure of **Florida town storytelling**: a setting warm enough to invite readers in, with just enough local memory, personality, and gossip to make a mystery matter.

For cozy mystery readers, a small town is never merely a backdrop. It is a living collection of neighbors, old grudges, rescue pets, community events, and unofficial experts who have opinions about everything from zoning changes to who makes the best key lime pie. Add a clever dog with a sensitive nose, and even a quiet afternoon may turn up a clue.

## Florida Town Storytelling Starts With a Sense of Place

Florida is often reduced to beaches, theme parks, and postcards full of palm trees. Those things certainly belong here, but they are only part of the picture. A town near an inland lake has a different rhythm from a Gulf Coast fishing community. An old railroad town feels different from a neighborhood built around citrus groves, horse farms, or a historic downtown square.

The most memorable stories use those distinctions. Maybe the town library occupies a former train depot. Maybe a century-old hotel has survived hurricanes, changing ownership, and a few suspicious legends. Maybe the annual seafood festival brings in enough visitors to make a missing person difficult to spot - or a stolen antique easy to hide.

A good setting gives characters something to react to. Summer heat can make tempers shorter. A sudden thunderstorm can send witnesses scurrying indoors. Hurricane preparation may reveal which neighbors show up with bottled water and plywood, and which ones have something to conceal. These details should serve the plot, not crowd it, but they make the story feel rooted in a real place.

## The Best Small Towns Have Long Memories

In a large city, a person can disappear into the crowd. In a small Florida town, a new haircut may be noticed before lunch. That closeness brings comfort, but it also brings complications. People remember high school rivalries, old business disputes, family scandals, and the one unfortunate incident at the charity auction ten years ago.

That long memory is a gift to a mystery writer. A crime in the present can have its roots in an old land deal, a vanished family heirloom, or a friendship that broke apart years earlier. Historical tidbits are especially useful when they do more than decorate the scene. The date on a town monument, a closed-off room in an old building, or a name repeated in cemetery records can quietly point toward the truth.

Still, small-town life should not be treated as a collection of nosy stereotypes. The people who ask too many questions may also bring soup when someone is sick, look after a neighbor's cat, or organize a fundraiser without being asked. Their concern can be genuine even when their methods are a little enthusiastic. That mixture of kindness and curiosity is where cozy mysteries find much of their heart.

### Familiar Faces Make the Stakes Personal

When readers return to the same town book after book, they want more than a new suspect list. They want to check in on familiar faces. Has the bakery owner finally taken a vacation? Is the town council still arguing about the old theater? Did the veterinarian's assistant adopt that mischievous kitten?

Recurring characters create a sense that life continues between mysteries. They also make danger feel more personal. If the person in trouble is someone readers have shared pancakes, parades, and pet-adoption days with, the case is no longer just an interesting puzzle. It is a problem that needs solving before the town's sense of safety is damaged.

That is one reason a canine narrator can be such a joyful guide. Dogs do not care who is wealthy, well-connected, or trying to impress the mayor. They notice nervous voices, unfamiliar scents, altered routines, and who slipped out the back door. In the Doc and Daisy Mysteries, Daisy's warm snout and sharp observations bring a playful angle to the clues while keeping the people around her very human.

## Why Dogs Belong in Florida Town Mysteries

Dogs naturally connect a town. They meet people on sidewalks, at parks, in veterinary offices, and outside cafes where someone has thoughtfully placed a water bowl. A dog may recognize the scent of a visitor before the humans do. She may also understand that a person who says, “Nothing is wrong,” does not smell quite as calm as they sound.

Canine forensics works best when it honors both the limits and gifts of a dog's senses. A dog can detect a scent trail, alert to a hidden object, or react to a familiar smell in an unfamiliar place. But a dog cannot explain every clue in a neat paragraph, and that is part of the fun. The human sleuth must interpret what the dog has found, test assumptions, and avoid leaping to conclusions just because someone was carrying bacon.

A veterinarian's perspective adds another layer. Animals often notice changes before people do, and their care can bring all kinds of residents through one door. A lost pet, an injured bird, an anxious horse, or a suspiciously ill show dog can open a path into the community. It also creates a natural foundation of compassion. The mystery may be lighthearted, but the care for animals should feel sincere.

## The Cozy Balance: Sunshine, Shadows, and Smart Clues

A Florida setting can be bright and cheerful without making every story sweet as orange marmalade. The best cozy mysteries make room for real motives: jealousy, greed, grief, fear, and the mistakes people make when they believe nobody is watching. The difference is in the treatment. Readers come for the puzzle and the company, not for graphic violence or despair.

That balance depends on tone. A funny moment should not erase a character's loss. A dangerous discovery should have consequences, even if the sleuth finds it while wearing flip-flops and carrying a bag of dog treats. Humor works because it grows from character: the retired neighbor who has a theory for everything, the cat who chooses the worst possible moment to sit on an important document, or the dog who knows a snack opportunity when she sees one.

The clues need to be fair, too. Readers enjoy being surprised, but they also want the satisfaction of realizing the answer was in front of them. A seemingly ordinary conversation at the farmers market, a contradiction in a local-history tale, or a muddy paw print near a locked gate can all become meaningful later. Modern twists such as digital messages, security cameras, and online rumors can add complications, but they should not replace careful observation.

## What Readers Carry Away From a Florida Town Story

The lasting appeal is not only the solution to the crime. It is the feeling of having visited a place where people know the streets, care about the animals, and show up when trouble arrives. Florida offers plenty of color and contradiction for this kind of story: old and new, wild and carefully manicured, peaceful mornings and dramatic weather by late afternoon.

A fictional town does not need to be perfect to be welcoming. In fact, its quirks are what make it believable. Let the local diner run out of pie. Let the town sign have a misspelled word nobody has bothered to fix. Let one neighbor know every secret and another be determined to prove them wrong. Then give readers a sleuth with common sense, a good heart, and perhaps a canine partner who knows that every investigation goes better after a walk.

The next time you open a cozy mystery set in a Florida town, pay attention to the details that make you linger: the old stories, the friendly faces, the suspicious footprints, and the dog waiting patiently beside the clue. That is where a town begins to feel like somewhere worth returning to.

What is Downgrading Trump’s Presidency?

Was it the Iran war or overambitious tariffs that triggered inflation and damaged President Trump’s presidency? It was a combination of these and several other policy failures. 

Domestically, inflation and ICE excesses badly tarnished his image. If we look back his presidency, six years, Trump was not the politician we see him today. His defeat in 2020 pushed him closer to ultra-conservatives, whose influence reshaped his outlook. They surrounded him with incompetent but fiercely loyal advisers and cabinet members, all committed to advancing the MAGA agenda. What was supposed to deliver a stronger America has instead produced a political debacle.

Trump’s honeymoon is over. The midterm voters have rejected his policies, costing Republicans their majorities in both houses of Congress. 

His political troubles are far from over. The controversy surrounding Defence Secretary Hegseth and the threat of impeachment may have been temporarily stalled, but a heavily Democratic Congress is unlikely to let the matter rest. To limit further political damage, Trump may eventually have to replace him with a more competent figure.

Tariffs and Inflation: A Self-Inflicted Wound.

Tariffs and inflation became everyday concerns in American households. Trump promised that import duties would fill government coffers with billions of dollars while protecting American industry. 

The reality was quite different. Courts blocked much of his tariff programme, forcing him to use emergency powers to restore some duties. Meanwhile, foreign exporters raised prices to offset the tariffs, leaving American importers and consumers to bear much of the cost. The Treasury collected less than promised, while consumers faced higher prices. Trump had created an economic and political disaster for himself.

Iran War: The Biggest Strategic Miscalculation
Trump became overconfident after the relatively quick operation in Venezuela, where control over its oil resources appeared to offer a political victory. He seemingly believed Iran could be dealt with in much the same way. 

Under the pretext of stopping its nuclear ambitions, he launched a bombing campaign, overlooking the strategic consequences.

Iran survived the attacks and retaliated through the one weapon it could effectively deploy: disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The resulting surge in global oil prices hurt economies worldwide, including America’s. Whatever damage tariffs had not caused, the unfinished Iran war compounded. With no clear resolution in sight, the conflict became another major liability for Trump.

ICE Excesses: Losing Public Sympathy

The aggressive ICE crackdown also damaged his standing. Illegal immigrants working in low-paid jobs, often shunned by American workers, were rounded up, detained and deported. While many Americans have limited sympathy for illegal immigration, they strongly objected to the heavy-handed methods. The excesses in Minnesota became a particularly damaging example. Public resistance grew, adding another burden to an already unpopular presidency.

Trump now has two years left in office. The midterm verdict should be a wake-up call. Unless he changes his approach, replaces poor advisers and rethinks his policies, he risks turning the remainder of his presidency into a prolonged political decline.

text:
HSE Allows Minors Abortion Without Parental Knowledge

Should a Parent Be Informed and Have Input?

Official HSE guidance allows teenagers as young as 15, and in some cases younger, to be offered an abortion without their parents’ knowledge or consent. For 16 and 17-year-olds, a doctor may proceed if satisfied the young person understands the information and can give valid consent. 

For those aged 15 or under, the same is possible “if there are exceptional circumstances and an assessment has been completed.” Parents are merely “encouraged” to be involved, they are not required to be informed.

This policy has been public since 2019. It appears in HSE booklets on medical and surgical abortion and on the HSE website. Doctors must still report certain cases to Tusla, but these obligations do not require informing parents of the abortion itself. Ending a pregnancy is not a routine medical procedure. It is permanent, carries physical and psychological risks, and for a minor raises serious questions of maturity, coercion, and long-term consequences. 

In almost every other area of significant medical decision-making for children under 16, Irish law and HSE policy default to parental involvement. The statutory right of those over 16 to consent to treatment does not automatically justify treating abortion as uniquely exempt from ordinary safeguards for younger teenagers. “Exceptional circumstances” remains entirely undefined in public HSE materials. No clear criteria or transparent process exist, leaving wide discretion to individual doctors with little external accountability. 

Supporters argue that mandatory notification could endanger girls in abusive homes. Those risks are real. Child-protection law already exists for such cases: Tusla can intervene where there is evidence of abuse or risk. The difficulty is that the guidance does not limit non-notification to suspected abuse. It allows secrecy based on the minor’s preference and a doctor’s assessment of capacity, even in the absence of protective concerns.

Capacity is not a binary switch. Many 15 and 16-year-olds lack the life experience and future-oriented judgment to fully weigh a decision of this magnitude under the pressure of an unplanned pregnancy. Parents remain legally accountable for their children’s welfare. 
A system that systematically excludes them from a decision this consequential, while still holding them responsible afterwards, creates a clear inconsistency.The presumption should be that parents are informed and involved, with narrow, defined, and reviewable exceptions only where notification would place the child at risk of serious harm.

 “Exceptional circumstances” should be specified and subject to oversight rather than left to individual discretion. Parents are not bystanders. On a decision this significant, they should not be treated as optional.
So Should a parent be informed and have input?
