text:
$IIIV Q4 2026 earnings: i3 Verticals cloud subscriptions rise, but its underlying sales shrink

i3 Verticals, a provider of software and payment systems to state and local governments, grew its cloud subscriptions while its older revenue streams shrank. Fourth-quarter revenue edged up 1% to $55 million, but by our math sales from businesses owned a year ago fell 3% once the January insurance software acquisition is removed. Chief executive Greg Daily pointed to 7% recurring revenue growth and wider operating margins, while heavy share buybacks lifted per-share profit excluding one-offs to $0.30, above what the company's own plan pointed to.

• Sales from businesses owned a year ago: -𝟑% (by our math; +1% reported ($55.4M))
• Annualized recurring revenue: $𝟏𝟕𝟕.𝟎𝐌 (+7% reported; +2% underlying by our math)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟎.𝟑𝟎 (+11% from a year ago on 23% fewer shares)
• FY27 revenue outlook: $𝟐𝟐𝟎–𝟐𝟑𝟓𝐌 (middle of the range: 4% growth (below 4–6% prior view))

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because underlying recurring revenue slowed again and the new 2027 revenue plan sits below the mid-single-digit growth pace management indicated last quarter. Transaction fees stalled after three quarters of growth, maintenance revenue fell more than twice as fast as planned, and debt-funded buybacks will push cash interest costs up 68% in 2027. The good news: the company cut direct service costs, raised its acquisition payout estimates—a sign the January deal is performing well—and settled the Louisiana cybersecurity lawsuit for $3 million net of insurance.

The question now is whether cloud software rollouts add enough net new spending to lift underlying growth, or merely replace shrinking maintenance and service fees while interest costs climb. If new state transportation and court contracts add net revenue, recurring growth will hold near 7% after the January acquisition enters the comparison base; if they mostly convert existing clients, total growth will slip toward 2%. Second-quarter 2027 recurring revenue will settle it.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬
i3 Verticals sells software and payment systems to state and local governments. Even though fourth-quarter sales rose only 1%, the company expanded its operating profit margin excluding one-offs by 1.2 percentage points to 27.4%. It cut its costs of services—the direct expense of hosting and supporting software—by 2.5 percentage points of revenue to 29.7%, which more than offset a 2.0-point rise in recurring overhead and software expenses.

Separately, the public-sector software provider recorded a $6.1 million non-cash charge for "changes in management’s estimates of future cash consideration to be paid in connection with prior acquisitions". Because the January 2026 motor-vehicle insurance software acquisition carries up to $20 million in performance payouts, a higher payout estimate suggests that acquired business is hitting its growth targets.

What to watch: the annual report's acquisition footnote. It will confirm whether the $6.1 million earn-out adjustment came from the January insurance software deal outperforming its initial plan.

🟢 concern eased — 𝐋𝐨𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐚 𝐋𝐚𝐰𝐬𝐮𝐢𝐭 𝐒𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐅𝐨𝐫 $𝟑 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐍𝐞𝐭
A long-running cybersecurity lawsuit in Louisiana had threatened the government software vendor with an uncertain legal bill after plaintiffs filed a sealed claim for damages well above $22 million. This quarter, i3 Verticals accrued a $3.0 million expense "for the expected settlement of the lawsuit State of Louisiana, et al. v. i3-Software & Services, LLC, et al.".

That $3.0 million figure is the company's net cost "excluding amounts expected to be paid directly by insurance". Resolving the case for a capped $3 million cash outlay removes a major balance-sheet risk for a business that generated $44.8 million in full-year free cash flow by our math.

What to watch: the legal proceedings footnote in the upcoming annual filing. Final court approval of the settlement agreement will close this liability permanently.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭
Several operational milestones and artificial intelligence product rollouts had no new numbers in the fourth-quarter press release because management reports them on the conference call or in the annual filing.

• Court software rollouts: whether the company brought two promised court customers live on its new integration tool during the fourth quarter.
• Artificial intelligence contracts: contract values and revenue timing for the eight government document-processing deals announced last quarter.
• Card processing costs: whether management completed its planned fourth-quarter fix with its payment processor to lower commercial-card fees.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐮𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐦 𝐂𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐦𝐬
"We closed fiscal 2026 with strong momentum, highlighted by 7% recurring revenue growth and more than 100 basis points of adjusted EBITDA margin expansion," chief executive Greg Daily said. Daily added that "We enter fiscal 2027 positioned for accelerating organic growth and margin improvement." Annualized recurring revenue (ARR)—quarterly revenue from ongoing contracts multiplied by four—reached $177.0 million, up 7.1% from a year ago.

The numbers tell a weaker story once the January 2026 insurance software acquisition is stripped out. Using the $2.3 million quarterly run-rate disclosed in the prior filing, sales from businesses owned a year ago fell about 3.2% in the fourth quarter by our math, worse than the 2% decline in the third quarter. By the same math, underlying ARR grew less than 2%.

The new 2027 revenue outlook of $220 million to $235 million points to 4.0% total growth at the middle of the range, or about 3.0% excluding the first-quarter acquisition benefit by our math. That falls below the 4% to 6% pace management pointed to just three months ago.

What to watch: annualized recurring revenue growth in the second quarter of fiscal 2027. Once the January acquisition enters the year-ago comparison base, reported recurring growth will show the true underlying pace.

🔴🔴 𝐌𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐀𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦𝐬 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐮𝐭 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐮𝐝 𝐆𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬
i3 Verticals is moving government customers to software-as-a-service (SaaS), where clients pay a subscription to access cloud software. While cloud subscription revenue jumped 35.0% from a year ago—helped by the January acquisition—older revenue streams weakened across the board.

• Software maintenance (ongoing support for installed systems): $7.3 million, down 8.6% from a year ago vs the 3.5% decline management told investors to expect.
• Transaction-based revenue (fees per payment, court filing, or utility bill): $19.9 million, down 0.2% after growing 12%, 7%, and 5% in the prior three quarters.
• Professional services (one-time installation and training): $8.5 million, down 26.2% against a tough year-ago comparison.

Because existing customers moving to the cloud stop paying maintenance fees, part of the cloud gain simply replaces lost maintenance revenue. Meanwhile, the stall in transaction fees removes a growth engine that previously made up over a third of total sales.

What to watch: transaction-based revenue growth in the first quarter. A second straight flat reading would confirm that slower payment and filing volume is a lasting drag rather than a one-quarter dip.

🔴 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭-𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐄𝐏𝐒 𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬
Management has used share buybacks to drive per-share profit growth while underlying earnings shrink. In the fourth quarter, profit per share excluding one-offs rose 11.1% to $0.30, beating the $0.25 to $0.29 range implied by the full-year outlook. Yet net income excluding one-offs actually fell 13.9% to $7.8 million.

A 22.7% drop in the diluted share count—to 26.4 million shares from 34.2 million a year ago—did all the work. To fund those buybacks and the January acquisition, the Nashville-based company drained its cash from $66.7 million to $3.7 million and drew $118.5 million on its credit line. That new debt carries a growing cost: the 2027 plan has cash interest expense jumping 68% at the midpoint to between $6 million and $8 million.

What to watch: quarterly net debt and share count in the first quarter. With net debt now at 1.9 times operating cash profit by our math, further borrowing to buy back shares will eat into the 2027 profit recovery.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐰𝐞𝐝 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐒𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐝
On October 9, 2026, i3 Verticals replaced its 2023 credit line with a new $350 million revolving credit facility led by JPMorgan Chase. The agreement caps total debt at 4.0 times operating cash profit and trims the interest rate spread by 0.50 percentage points, saving the company roughly $600,000 a year in interest on its current $118.5 million debt balance by our math.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟑𝟐.𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Deferred revenue—cash customers have paid in advance for software and support not yet delivered—fell 14.7% from $37.7 million a year ago, though it rose from $25.3 million in the third quarter on normal school-year billing. The year-over-year drop reflects customers moving away from annual-in-advance maintenance contracts.

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟏𝟑.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Free cash flow—operating cash flow minus computer equipment and software development spending—rose 19.5% from $11.7 million a year ago, reaching 25.1% of revenue. After dipping to $7.2 million in the second quarter and $10.8 million in the third, fourth-quarter cash generation benefited from tighter receivables collection.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞, 𝐧𝐞𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟓𝟒.𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Uncollected customer bills fell 6.6% from $58.5 million a year ago even as fourth-quarter revenue edged up 1.0%. Shrinking receivables show the public-sector vendor collected cash faster from government clients at year-end, helping lift fourth-quarter operating cash flow to $17.3 million.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟐𝟐𝟎.𝟎–𝟐𝟑𝟓.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from Mid-single-digit growth (~4–6%)
Cut. The middle of the new range ($227.5 million) equals 4.0% growth over fiscal 2026, sitting at the bottom of the mid-single-digit target management gave last quarter. By our math, stripping out one quarter of inorganic lift from the January 2026 acquisition leaves underlying sales growth of about 3.0%, after the company cut its 2026 revenue plan twice during the past year.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟔𝟏.𝟐𝟓–𝟔𝟖.𝟕𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. The plan calls for operating cash profit excluding one-offs to grow 10.7% at the $65.0 million midpoint, up from 2.0% growth in fiscal 2026. By our math, that puts the full-year margin at 28.6% at the middle of the ranges, a 1.7-percentage-point step-up from 26.8% in fiscal 2026.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐏𝐒: $𝟏.𝟐𝟑–𝟏.𝟒𝟏  ⇗ accelerating
New. The public-sector software group forecasts per-share profit excluding one-offs to rise 18.9% at the $1.32 midpoint, assuming a 25% tax rate. Because full-year share count already sits 11% higher than the fourth-quarter exit rate of 26.4 million shares, most of the planned per-share gain comes from buybacks already completed in 2026.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞: $𝟔.𝟎–𝟖.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. The outlook expects cash interest costs to climb 68.4% at the $7.0 million midpoint from $4.2 million in fiscal 2026. That increase reflects a full year of carrying the $118.5 million credit-line balance drawn down during 2026 for share repurchases and acquisitions, even after the 0.50-point rate cut on the new facility.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟏𝟎.𝟎–𝟏𝟐.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
New. Management plans for $11.0 million at the middle of the range, up 4.2% from $10.6 million in fiscal 2026. The steady expense line tracks capitalized software development spending, which totaled $9.5 million across the four quarters of fiscal 2026.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐉𝐚𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐚𝐜𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧?
Reported annualized recurring revenue grew 7.1%, but our math suggests underlying growth slowed below 2% once the insurance software acquisition is removed. Investors need the exact organic figure to judge the 2027 growth bridge.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧-𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐨 𝐚 𝟎.𝟐% 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞?
Transaction fees are the company's largest revenue stream at 36% of sales, and growth slowed from 12% in the first quarter to slightly negative in the fourth. Management has not explained whether volume or pricing drove the stop.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐬𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝟖.𝟔% 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐚 𝟑.𝟓% 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐭?
Three months ago the finance chief said maintenance declines would moderate to 3.5% going forward, yet the stream fell 8.6% in the fourth quarter. Clarifying how much of that drop converted into cloud subscriptions will show the net revenue gain.

𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭 𝐜𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐠𝐨 𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐥?
Management committed to bringing two court customers live on its artificial-intelligence integration framework in the fourth quarter, with a third right behind. The earnings release gave no update on those rollouts or on the delayed utility project.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐒𝐜𝐡𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧-𝐟𝐞𝐞 𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐬𝐮𝐢𝐭?
While the $3 million accrual settles the Louisiana cybersecurity case, the release did not mention the PaySchools class-action lawsuit, where plaintiffs were given leave to amend a challenge to the company's transaction-fee model.

text:
A MOUSE, A TIGER & A TOUCH OF MAGIC! 🎭

════════════ ❧ ════════════

CULTURAL DEBUTS 🎭

════════════ ❧ ════════════

A CULTURAL TIME CAPSULE ⋆ NOVEMBER 18 EDITION

════════════ ❧ ════════════

🕒 ESTIMATED READING TIME: 14–16 MINUTES

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🎵 Music ⋆ 📺 Television ⋆ 🎬 Film & Animation ⋆ 📚 Publishing & Literature ⋆ 🎭 Theatre ⋆ 📻 Radio ⋆ 🎮 Games & Other Cultural Firsts

──────────── ◈ ────────────

📜 EPIGRAPH

“Every author, as far as he is great and at the same time original, has had the task of creating the taste by which he is to be enjoyed.” — William Wordsworth, 1815.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🎭 THE CURTAIN RISES. THE CLOCK TURNS BACK. THE MAGIC BEGINS!

“Animation can explain whatever the mind of man can conceive.” — Walt Disney.

Some days don’t just mark the calendar—they detonate. They crash in with a roar, a gasp, a spotlight, or a tiny invention that rewires the ordinary forever.

Today is one of those days. A rock band tore itself apart and rebuilt itself in a city rising from the rubble, reinventing its entire sound. An unforgettable acoustic performance stripped a generation-defining group bare and showed the world a side no one had ever heard. Television screens flickered to life with a shape-shifting nightmare and a fearless trio of pint-sized superheroes. A mischievous mouse stepped into the spotlight and rewrote movie history. A monumental epic hauled ancient Rome onto the screen in all its brutal, breathtaking glory. A boy and his tiger wandered onto the comics page and stayed forever. Broadway welcomed a charming musical that transformed a working-class shop girl into a world of high fashion and romance. And a brand-new kind of telephone quietly asked the world to stop turning a dial and start pressing buttons—changing the way we talk, one click at a time.

FROM THE RECORD PLAYER TO THE TELEVISION SCREEN, FROM THE THEATRE TO THE ARCADE—LET US OPEN TODAY'S CULTURAL TIME CAPSULE! ✨

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🎵 MUSIC

1991 — U2 Releases Achtung Baby 🎸

On November 18, 1991, U2 released Achtung Baby, the band's seventh studio album, marking a dramatic change in its musical direction and visual identity.

Recorded primarily at Hansa Studios in Berlin and at other locations in Ireland, the album was produced by Daniel Lanois and Brian Eno. Its 12 tracks included “One,” “The Fly,” “Mysterious Ways,” “Until the End of the World,” and “Even Better Than the Real Thing.”

After the earnest, expansive sound of The Joshua Tree and the more roots-oriented Rattle and Hum, the band entered the early 1990s determined to challenge its own identity. Electronic textures, dance rhythms, distorted guitars, and layered production replaced much of the familiar sound. The result was not a retreat from U2's past but a bold reinvention.

Achtung Baby became a major commercial and critical success, reaching No. 1 in the United States and winning the Grammy Award for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal. It also laid the groundwork for the ambitious Zoo TV Tour, which turned the album's themes of media overload, spectacle, and modern identity into a multimedia concert experience.

🧩 TRIVIA: The album's title came from a phrase sound engineer Joe O'Herlihy used during the Berlin sessions. U2 had borrowed it from Mel Brooks's film The Producers.

🐶 SPOT: “One,” now one of U2's most enduring songs, emerged during a difficult writing period in Berlin. The band had reached an impasse, and the song took shape during a jam that helped the members rediscover a shared musical direction.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Reinvention can be an act of survival. Sometimes artists move forward by daring to become unfamiliar—even to themselves.

───────────────

1993 — Nirvana Records MTV Unplugged in New York 🎙️

On November 18, 1993, Nirvana recorded its now-legendary MTV Unplugged performance at Sony Music Studios in New York City.

Rather than delivering a conventional acoustic version of a greatest-hits concert, Kurt Cobain, Krist Novoselic, Dave Grohl, and guitarist Pat Smear built a set that mixed Nirvana songs with carefully chosen covers. The performance included “About a Girl,” “Come as You Are,” “All Apologies,” and “Pennyroyal Tea,” alongside songs associated with David Bowie, the Vaselines, and Lead Belly.

The Meat Puppets' Curt and Cris Kirkwood joined the band for three of their songs: “Plateau,” “Oh, Me,” and “Lake of Fire.” Cellist Lori Goldston added another dimension to the arrangements. The set's intimate atmosphere, unusual song choices, flowers, candles, and restrained staging created a performance unlike the explosive image many viewers associated with Nirvana.

The program aired on MTV in December 1993. Released as an album the following year, MTV Unplugged in New York became a posthumous landmark after Cobain's death in April 1994. It won the Grammy Award for Best Alternative Music Performance and offered listeners a revealing final chapter in the band's story.

🧩 TRIVIA: The performance included 14 songs, and six were covers. Nirvana did not use the occasion simply to replay its biggest hits.

🐶 SPOT: The three songs with the Meat Puppets were not casual guest appearances. Curt Kirkwood played guitar and Cris Kirkwood played bass, bringing the original band's own musicians into the performance.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: An artist's quietest performance can sometimes reveal more than the loudest one.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

📺 TELEVISION

1990 — Stephen King's It Premieres on ABC 🎈

On November 18, 1990, ABC aired the first part of It, its two-part television adaptation of Stephen King's 1986 horror novel.

Directed by Tommy Lee Wallace, the miniseries starred Richard Thomas as adult Bill Denbrough, John Ritter as Ben Hanscom, Annette O'Toole as Beverly Marsh, and Tim Curry as the terrifying Pennywise. The story follows a group of childhood friends who reunite in their hometown when a malevolent presence they encountered as children returns.

The production moved between two timelines, showing the characters first as children and later as adults. Its central terror was a creature capable of taking the form of whatever its victims feared most. For many viewers, however, the most unforgettable image was Curry's clown: playful on the surface, deeply menacing underneath.

The second part followed on November 20. The adaptation became one of the most recognizable television horror events of its era and introduced a generation of viewers to a screen version of King's monstrous creation.

🧩 TRIVIA: The Paley Center for Media archives the first installment with a running time of 1 hour and 55 minutes.

🐶 SPOT: Tim Curry's Pennywise became so closely associated with the character that the performance helped define how an entire generation pictured the novel's supernatural villain—even though the creature in King's story can take many forms.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The most frightening monster may not be the one with the sharpest teeth. It may be the one that knows exactly what scares you.

───────────────

1998 — The Powerpuff Girls Debut on Cartoon Network 💥

On November 18, 1998, Cartoon Network premiered The Powerpuff Girls, the animated series created by Craig McCracken.

The show followed Blossom, Bubbles, and Buttercup—three kindergarten-aged superheroes created in a laboratory by Professor Utonium. Despite their small size and childlike lives, the girls defended the fictional city of Townsville from an extraordinary collection of villains, monsters, and mischievous troublemakers.

The series combined bright, graphic animation with fast-paced action, absurd comedy, and affectionate parodies of superhero conventions. Its three heroines were deliberately different: Blossom was the strategist, Bubbles the sweet-natured optimist, and Buttercup the tough fighter. Their contrasting personalities gave the show much of its energy.

The characters had developed from McCracken's student work at CalArts, and the series became one of Cartoon Network's first major global franchise successes. It earned critical recognition, merchandise, feature-film treatment, and a lasting place in late-1990s animation.

🧩 TRIVIA: Before the television series, McCracken conceived the trio as The Whoopass Girls while studying at CalArts. The name was changed before the characters reached Cartoon Network.

🐶 SPOT: The three heroines were not designed as miniature versions of adult superheroes. Their kindergarten age was central to the joke and the show's appeal: they could save the world and still have to deal with bedtime, school, and sibling-style arguments.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A fresh idea can turn an unlikely combination—in this case, preschool innocence and superhero action—into a cultural phenomenon.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🎬 FILM & ANIMATION

1928 — Steamboat Willie Introduces Mickey and Minnie Mouse 🚢

On November 18, 1928, Walt Disney's Steamboat Willie premiered at New York City's Colony Theatre, introducing Mickey and Minnie Mouse to movie audiences.

Directed by Walt Disney and animated principally by Ub Iwerks, the black-and-white short follows Mickey as a mischievous deckhand aboard a steamboat captained by the intimidating Pete. Minnie joins him, and the pair turn the boat's equipment—and even its animals—into an improvised musical performance.

The cartoon became a landmark because its sound was synchronized with the action. Music, whistles, squeaks, and effects were timed to the movement on screen, creating a lively relationship between image and soundtrack at a moment when synchronized sound was transforming motion pictures.

The short was not the first Mickey cartoon made. Plane Crazy had been completed and shown in a test screening earlier in 1928, but it failed to secure distribution. Steamboat Willie was the first Mickey Mouse cartoon released to the public, and its success helped launch one of the most recognizable characters in entertainment history.

🧩 TRIVIA: Mickey's official birthday is celebrated on November 18 because that is the date Steamboat Willie premiered in 1928. Minnie Mouse shares the same screen debut.

🐶 SPOT: After an unsuccessful early recording attempt, Disney used the Powers Cinephone process and recorded the soundtrack with a 15-piece band. Walt Disney supplied Mickey's squeaks himself, helping turn the character's movements into part of the music.

🔑 ESOTERIC: The film's title and riverboat setting drew on the popular 1928 Buster Keaton film Steamboat Bill, Jr. The cartoon was a comic parody, not an unrelated river adventure.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A cultural icon can begin with a few minutes of animation—and a new way of making audiences hear what they see.

───────────────

1959 — Ben-Hur Makes Its World Premiere 🏛️

On November 18, 1959, William Wyler's Ben-Hur held its world premiere in New York City, launching one of the most ambitious productions in Hollywood history.

Based on Lew Wallace's 1880 novel Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ, the film starred Charlton Heston as Judah Ben-Hur, a Jewish prince betrayed by his childhood friend Messala, played by Stephen Boyd. The story follows Judah's struggle for survival, revenge, and eventual spiritual transformation during the Roman occupation of Judea.

Produced by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, the film was a monumental undertaking. Its scale, elaborate sets, large cast, and sweeping locations gave audiences an epic spectacle, but its emotional center remained a story of friendship, betrayal, suffering, and forgiveness.

The famous chariot race became one of cinema's most celebrated action sequences. The film went on to win 11 Academy Awards from 12 nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Actor for Heston—a record-setting total at the time.

🧩 TRIVIA: The AFI Catalog lists the film's running time at 212 minutes, making it one of the longest major Hollywood productions of its era.

🐶 SPOT: The New York premiere came before the Los Angeles premiere, which was held on November 24, 1959, as a benefit for the University of Southern California Medical School Scholarship Fund.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The grandest spectacle works best when it carries a human story large enough to match its scale.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

📚 PUBLISHING & LITERATURE

1985 — Calvin and Hobbes Debuts in Newspaper Comics 🐯

On November 18, 1985, Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes made its newspaper debut, introducing readers to a mischievous six-year-old boy and his tiger companion.

The first strip opened with Calvin explaining to his father that he had set a tiger trap. In the final panel, Hobbes is revealed happily eating the tuna sandwich used as bait. That simple introduction established the comic's playful uncertainty: to Calvin, Hobbes was a living, talking tiger; to everyone else, he appeared to be a stuffed toy.

Watterson used the boy-and-tiger friendship to explore childhood imagination, family life, school, consumer culture, philosophy, and the absurdities of adult behavior. The strip's humor could be slapstick one day and unexpectedly thoughtful the next. Its visual imagination and literary references helped it appeal to children and adults alike.

The strip began in newspapers across the country. By the end of its run on December 31, 1995, it appeared in more than 2,400 newspapers. Watterson ended it at the height of its popularity, choosing to conclude the story on his own terms.

🧩 TRIVIA: Calvin is named after theologian John Calvin, while Hobbes takes his name from philosopher Thomas Hobbes—an intellectual joke tucked inside a comic strip about a six-year-old and his tiger.

🐶 SPOT: Watterson famously resisted commercial licensing, refusing to turn his characters into a sprawling merchandise franchise. He believed that keeping the strip focused on the work itself helped protect its creative independence.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Imagination can make an ordinary childhood world feel limitless—and sometimes the best way to preserve a creation is to know when to let it end.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🎭 THEATRE

1919 — Irene Opens on Broadway 👗

On November 18, 1919, the musical Irene opened at Broadway's Vanderbilt Theatre, introducing audiences to the story of a working-class shop girl whose life changes after she enters the world of wealth and high fashion.

With a book by James Montgomery, music by Harry Tierney, and lyrics by Joseph McCarthy, the production starred Edith Day in the title role. The story followed Irene O'Dare, an Irish American shop girl from New York's working-class Ninth Avenue, who is transformed into a society beauty and catches the attention of wealthy Donald Marshall.

The musical's appeal rested on a Cinderella-like story, lively songs, and the fantasy of social reinvention. Its most enduring number, “Alice Blue Gown,” became closely associated with the production.

Irene ran for 675 performances, an extraordinary achievement for its era, and became one of Broadway's major musical hits of the early 20th century.

🧩 TRIVIA: A silent film adaptation starring Colleen Moore followed in 1926, carrying the Broadway musical's story from the stage to the screen.

🐶 SPOT: The original leading lady, Edith Day, later recreated the role in London and stayed there, becoming one of the West End's leading female musical performers.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A familiar story can become a theatrical sensation when it gives audiences a character whose hopes feel close to their own.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🎮 GAMES & OTHER CULTURAL FIRSTS

1963 — Touch-Tone Telephone Service Begins 📞

On November 18, 1963, Bell Telephone began offering the world's first commercial electronic push-button telephone service, initially in Carnegie and Greensburg, Pennsylvania.

The new system replaced the familiar rotary dial with buttons that sent combinations of electronic tones through the telephone network. Customers could enter numbers directly, making dialing faster and eliminating the need to rotate a dial for every digit.

The first Western Electric Touch-Tone sets had only 10 buttons: the numbers zero through nine. The familiar star and pound keys were added later. The service cost customers an additional fee, and its initial availability was limited to the two Pennsylvania communities.

The change seems ordinary today, but it represented a major step in the evolution of telecommunications. Touch-tone dialing eventually became essential to automated phone systems, voicemail, banking services, and the menu-driven telephone networks used around the world.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original Touch-Tone telephone had 10 buttons, not the 12-button keypad familiar today. The star and pound keys came later.

🐶 SPOT: Engineers tested 15 different keypad arrangements before settling on the layout that became familiar: three rows of numbers with zero centered beneath them.

🏆 FIRST: Carnegie and Greensburg, Pennsylvania, became the first communities to receive the commercial electronic Touch-Tone service on November 18, 1963.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Some of the most important cultural changes do not arrive as entertainment. They enter our daily routines so completely that we eventually forget life was ever different.

───────────────

1988 — Konami Releases Gyruss for Japan's Famicom Disk System 🕹️

On November 18, 1988, Konami released Gyruss for the Famicom Disk System in Japan, bringing its space-shooter action to Nintendo's disk-based home gaming platform.

The game places players in control of a spacecraft traveling through a circular field of space, firing at enemies that approach from the outer edge. Its distinctive tube-shooter perspective gives the action a sense of motion and depth, while the player rotates around the screen to line up shots and avoid incoming attacks.

Gyruss had already established itself as an arcade game earlier in the decade. The Famicom Disk System release brought the experience to Japanese home players, adapting the fast-moving action for a different format.

Its combination of familiar space-combat imagery and unusual circular movement made it stand apart from more conventional side-scrolling shooters.

🧩 TRIVIA: The November 18, 1988 date refers to the Japanese Famicom Disk System release—not the game's original arcade debut.

🐶 SPOT: Gyruss is often described as a “tube shooter” because enemies move around a circular playfield, giving players the sensation of firing through a tunnel toward the center.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A familiar genre can feel new again when a designer changes the way players see and move through the action.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

📚 SOURCES & FURTHER READING

🎵 MUSIC

🎮 GAMES & OTHER CULTURAL FIRSTS

📜 QUOTATIONS

Walt Disney — “Animation can explain whatever the mind of man can conceive.” — D23, Walt Disney quote archive.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

AND WHAT A SHOW IT HAS BEEN! 🎭

November 18 didn’t just mark a date—it detonated a cultural supernova.

U2 ripped open their own sound with Achtung Baby and dared to reinvent themselves, while Nirvana's MTV Unplugged in New York captured Kurt Cobain and his band delivering a raw, unfiltered performance that still echoes as one of the most unforgettable recordings ever committed to tape.

Television stared us down with Stephen King's shape-shifting nightmare It, brought to life by Tim Curry's terrifying Pennywise, then flipped the script with Craig McCracken's The Powerpuff Girls, handing the fate of Townsville to Blossom, Bubbles, and Buttercup—three pint-sized heroes who proved that courage doesn't come with a height requirement.

Walt Disney's Steamboat Willie introduced Mickey and Minnie Mouse to movie audiences and helped rewrite the rules of synchronized animation forever, while Charlton Heston's Ben-Hur thundered onto the screen and redefined what an epic could mean. Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes introduced the unforgettable friendship between a mischievous boy and his tiger, reminding us that the wildest adventures still live in the imagination. Meanwhile, Broadway welcomed Edith Day in Irene, a musical that turned a working-class shop girl's story into a theatrical sensation.

Somewhere in the middle of all that magic, Bell Telephone's Touch-Tone service introduced the push-button telephone, helping bury the rotary dial, while Konami's Gyruss brought its distinctive space-shooter action to the Japanese Famicom Disk System.

Different voices. Different stages. Different revolutions.
Yet every single one of them shouts the same electrifying truth: culture is never finished. It keeps exploding, evolving, challenging us, delighting us, and finding brand-new ways to pull us closer together.
What a day. What a legacy. What a reminder that the best is always still being born.

THE NEXT GREAT CULTURAL FIRST MAY BE JUST AROUND THE CORNER. ✨

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🍬 CANDY

A new device arrives with a promise that sounds almost impossible: a reader can carry an entire library in one hand, buy a book without visiting a store, and receive it wirelessly in less than a minute. No computer. No trip to the bookstore. Just a new chapter in the way people read.

What was the name of this groundbreaking electronic reader, and how many books could its first model store?

The Border Wars: Missouri and Kansas Take the Rivalry to the Air

Four receivers. Two states. More than 5,100 receiving yards.

The Border Wars started on the ground, where Kansas claimed the statistical edge in our running back comparison. Now it’s Missouri’s turn to answer.

For round two, Market Athletes is highlighting the top two receiving-yard producers from each state, based on the supplied 2026 MaxPreps figures.

Together, these four athletes recorded 5,104 receiving yards, 328 receptions, and 51 receiving touchdowns in their reported games. All four surpassed 1,000 yards—but each brings a different story to the matchup.

🏈 MISSOURI: VOLUME AND PRODUCTION

Carson Nestleroad | @MonettFootball | Senior

Nestleroad enters the Border Wars with the largest receiving-yard total of the group—and he did it in just 10 reported games.

The Monett senior finished with 1,599 receiving yards and 17 touchdowns on 97 receptions. That’s an average of 159.9 yards per game and 16.48 yards per catch.

His yardage, yards per game, and touchdown totals lead all four receivers in this matchup. He also recorded the longest reception of the group, an 80-yard play.

Nestleroad was a primary target in a Monett passing attack led by quarterback Dylan Washick. That connection will come back into focus later in the series when we turn our attention to the quarterbacks.

For now, Nestleroad gives Missouri a receiver whose combination of catches, yardage, and touchdowns sets a high bar for the rest of the field.

@TrevorHeman | @Glendale_FB | Senior

Nestleroad leads this group in yards, but Heman has a distinction of his own: nobody caught more passes.

The Glendale senior recorded 111 receptions for 1,385 yards and nine touchdowns across 11 reported games. He averaged 125.9 yards per game and 12.48 yards per reception.

That’s more than 10 catches per reported game—a workload that speaks to how often Heman was involved in Glendale’s passing attack. His 111 receptions give Missouri a second receiver who consistently produced on a large number of opportunities.

Heman’s season also adds to a career that, according to the supplied notes, has surpassed 3,000 receiving yards. He has received an offer from Missouri State.

🏈 KANSAS: BIG PLAYS AND SCORING

@CamRon5Fields | @WashHouseFB | Senior

Kansas answers with a receiver who made the most of his opportunities.

Fields recorded 57 catches for 1,072 yards and 14 touchdowns in 10 reported games. His 18.81 yards per reception lead all four athletes in this comparison, and his 14 touchdowns rank second only to Nestleroad.

Fields averaged 107.2 receiving yards per game and recorded a longest reception of 71 yards. He was also a contributor in the running game, adding another dimension to his role in Washington’s offense.

His production was part of a memorable season for the Wildcats. Washington finished 7-3 and earned the program’s first playoff win, according to the supplied notes.

Fields may have had fewer catches than either Missouri receiver, but his average per reception and touchdown total make his impact clear.

@coy_barta | @Seaman_Vikings | Senior

Barta gives Kansas another productive target with a knack for generating yards.

The Seaman senior finished with 63 receptions for 1,048 yards and 11 touchdowns in nine reported games. He averaged 116.4 yards per game and 16.64 yards per reception, with a longest catch of 76 yards.

One of his standout performances was a 267-yard outingas part of a productive connection with Seaman quarterback Cale Ketter.

Barta, an Emporia State commit, averaged nearly seven catches per reported game while clearing the 1,000-yard mark in fewer reported games than the other receivers featured.

🔥 WHO TAKES ROUND TWO?

In the rushing comparison, Kansas led the way in combined yards and touchdowns. This time, Missouri has the statistical edge in receiving yards.

Nestleroad and Heman combined for 2,984 receiving yards on 208 catches, compared with 2,120 yards on 120 catches for Fields and Barta. That gives Missouri an advantage of 864 yards across the players’ reported games.

The touchdown comparison is much closer: Missouri’s duo combined for 26 receiving touchdowns, while Kansas’ duo combined for 25.

Kansas also brings the matchup’s highest yards-per-catch average through Fields. Missouri’s receivers played in a combined 21 reported games to Kansas’ 19, and differences in offensive systems, schedules, and opportunities all add context to the totals.

On the numbers used for this series, Kansas takes rushing and Missouri answers in receiving.
That leaves one position group to settle the next debate: quarterbacks.

👇 Which receiving duo are you taking—Kansas or Missouri? Let us know in the comments.

Statistics are based on the supplied MaxPreps figures for the 2026 varsity season, current as of mid-November. Game counts reflect each player’s reported statistics.

My discussion with Grok about the American political party system and it's role in politics.  How do We the People fight such a beast?  I found Grok to be spot on, what you think?:

The presidency is selected, constrained, and largely defined by party structures. Individual ambition or reluctance is secondary to party calculation, convention dynamics, coalition management, and legislative support.

An examination of the parties is warranted. They are the primary mechanisms that have determined who reaches the office and what can be done once there. If you want to begin, we can start with their origins, their changing roles in nominating and constraining presidents, or any particular era that interests you.

**Origins of the American Political Parties**

The Constitution contains no mention of political parties. The framers, particularly Madison and Washington, viewed “factions” as dangerous to republican government and expected the system of separated powers and federalism to control them. Parties nevertheless emerged within the first decade of the new government because organized disagreement over fundamental questions proved unavoidable.

**The First Party System (c. 1790s–1810s)**

Two loose coalitions formed around the policies of the Washington and Adams administrations:

- **Federalists**, led by Alexander Hamilton and supported by John Adams, favored a strong national government, a national bank, assumption of state debts, protective tariffs, and close commercial ties with Britain. They drew support from commercial interests, creditors, and much of New England.
- **Democratic-Republicans** (often called Republicans), led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, opposed the bank and the assumption of state debts, favored strict construction of the Constitution, agrarian interests, and closer ties with revolutionary France. Their base was stronger in the South and among small farmers.

These were not yet modern parties. They lacked permanent national committees, formal platforms, or disciplined legislative caucuses. Organization was personal, local, and temporary—centered on newspapers, correspondence societies, and electoral tickets. The 1796 and 1800 elections were the first openly contested presidential contests. Jefferson’s victory in 1800 and the subsequent decline of the Federalists after the War of 1812 produced the “Era of Good Feelings,” a period of one-party dominance that proved temporary.

**Why Parties Formed**

Three structural features of the Constitution made parties almost inevitable:

1. The need to organize majorities in Congress and to win the Electoral College.
2. Persistent disagreements over the scope of national power, foreign policy, and the balance between commercial and agrarian interests.
3. The absence of any other mechanism for coordinating candidates and voters across states.

By the 1820s the old Jeffersonian coalition had fractured. The contested election of 1824 and the rise of Andrew Jackson produced the second party system, with Democrats and National Republicans (later Whigs) replacing the earlier Federalist–Republican alignment. That later development built on, rather than replaced, the institutional logic already visible in the 1790s: parties exist to win elections and to organize government under a constitutional system that otherwise provides no formal role for them.

The parties therefore began as practical responses to the demands of republican government, not as institutions contemplated by the framers. Their subsequent history is largely the story of how those original purposes expanded, professionalized, and came to dominate the selection and operation of the presidency.

The Electoral College is the constitutional mechanism that formally elects the president and vice president. It was designed as a mediated link between the people and the highest office, not as a direct popular vote and not as a pure legislative choice.

**Constitutional Design (Article II, Section 1, as amended by the 12th Amendment)**

Each state is allocated a number of electors equal to its total congressional representation: two senators plus the number of representatives in the House. The 23rd Amendment later gave the District of Columbia three electors. The total is currently 538; a majority of 270 is required to win.

The framers rejected both a pure national popular vote and election by Congress. They sought a temporary body of electors, chosen in the states, who would exercise independent judgment. In practice the system quickly became a vehicle for party tickets rather than independent deliberation.

**How Electors Are Chosen and Vote**

The Constitution leaves the method of choosing electors to each state legislature. By the 1830s almost every state had adopted popular election of electors. Today every state uses a popular vote within the state (or, in Maine and Nebraska, a district system). The candidate who wins the statewide popular vote normally receives all of that state’s electoral votes (the “winner-take-all” rule), except in the two states that allocate by congressional district.

Electors meet in their respective states in mid-December and cast separate ballots for president and vice president. The results are transmitted to Congress and counted in early January. If no candidate obtains a majority, the House of Representatives chooses the president (one vote per state delegation) and the Senate chooses the vice president.

**Relation to “the People”**

The Electoral College is the formal tie between popular voting and the presidency, but it is an indirect and state-based tie:

- Citizens vote for electors (or, in practice, for a party slate of electors) rather than directly for the presidential candidates.
- The weight of each citizen’s vote depends on the population and representation of his or her state.
- A candidate can win the national popular vote and still lose the Electoral College, and vice versa, because the system aggregates state results rather than raw national totals.

This structure was intentional. It preserved a role for the states as political communities, protected smaller states from being overwhelmed by larger ones, and required a candidate to assemble geographically distributed majorities. Over time the parties nationalized the contest, turning the Electoral College into a state-by-state competition for electoral votes rather than a deliberative body. The constitutional form, however, remains the same: the people choose electors; the electors choose the president.

That is the mechanism that has governed every presidential election since 1789.
Yes, that is a fair reading of the original constitutional design, though it is only part of the picture.

Under the Constitution the states are the primary political communities. The House is apportioned by population and elected by the people of the states; the Senate was originally chosen by the state legislatures (until the 17th Amendment); and the method of appointing presidential electors is left to each state legislature. The 10th Amendment reserves to the states or the people all powers not delegated to the national government. In that architecture the state legislatures were intended to be the ordinary and continuing voice of the people for most domestic purposes and the principal intermediaries for national action.

The Electoral College itself reflects this structure: the people act through their states, and the state legislatures decide how the people’s choice of electors is organized. The framers expected most governance, and most expression of popular will, to remain at the state level; the national government was to be limited to the enumerated powers.

That original expectation has been heavily modified in practice. The 17th Amendment removed the state legislatures from the selection of senators. The growth of national parties, the nationalization of the presidential campaign, the expansion of federal statutory and administrative power, and the rise of direct national media have all reduced the practical role of state legislatures as the ordinary national voice. They still control the mechanics of presidential elections within their states and retain substantial reserved powers, but they no longer function as the primary or exclusive channel for the people’s national representation.

So the statement is accurate as a description of the 1787–1791 design and of the formal role still assigned to state legislatures in the Electoral College. It is less accurate as a description of how national politics actually operates today.

Parties acquired public functions and legal privileges through a combination of political practice, state legislation, and judicial acceptance over roughly a century and a half. They did not receive them by constitutional grant.

**How the acquisition occurred**

- Early practice (1790s–1820s): Congressional caucuses and informal meetings nominated candidates. These were private gatherings; government merely printed the names the caucuses supplied.
- State legislation (mid-19th century onward): As the electorate expanded, states began regulating nominations to prevent fraud and chaos. They enacted laws that recognized party primaries, required parties to file candidate lists, and later mandated state-run primary elections. Once a party met a state’s ballot-access threshold, the state treated its nominees as the official party candidates. Those statutes converted private choices into public ballot status.
- Judicial reinforcement: Courts upheld the statutes. They treated parties as organizations that performed a public role in the electoral process and therefore could be regulated, while still regarding their internal rules as largely private. Key decisions confirmed that states could require primaries, set filing deadlines, and limit who appears on the general-election ballot.
- Federal layer: The Federal Election Campaign Act (1971 and later amendments) gave national party committees public financing options, higher contribution limits, and official status with the Federal Election Commission once they registered. Again, the privileges followed from statutes, not from the Constitution.

**Whose powers?**

The underlying constitutional powers—to set the qualifications of electors, to prescribe the times, places, and manner of congressional elections, and to appoint presidential electors—remain with the states and with Congress (Article I, Section 4; Article II, Section 1). Parties exercise no independent constitutional authority. They hold the practical advantages they do because legislatures have chosen to channel ballot access and public funding through party organizations, and because courts have sustained those choices.

Parties do not, in law, “become” the People. They are private associations that have been given preferential access to the public machinery of elections. The People retain the formal power to alter that arrangement through state legislatures, through Congress, or through constitutional amendment. Whether they will do so is a political question; the legal title to the power has never left the constitutional bodies that originally possessed it.

The incentive exists. A less-informed and less-attentive electorate lowers the cost of persuasion and reduces the risk that voters will punish parties for decisions that serve donors or institutional interests over broader public ones.

**How the incentive operates**

- **Information costs**: Detailed knowledge of legislation, budgets, regulatory capture, or foreign commitments requires time and effort. When most voters lack that knowledge, parties and their allied spenders can frame issues through short, emotional, or misleading messages that are cheaper to produce and harder to rebut.
- **Distraction**: Continuous focus on personality conflicts, cultural symbols, or short-term scandals crowds out scrutiny of structural questions—contribution rules, ballot-access barriers, appointment power, or the long-term effects of spending and debt. Both major parties benefit when those structural questions remain secondary.
- **Mobilization versus persuasion**: Parties need high turnout among their core supporters and low turnout or confusion among opponents. A distracted public is easier to segment, micro-target, and selectively mobilize; it is harder to assemble a sustained, cross-party majority around institutional reform.
- **Donor priority**: Large contributors care about specific, often technical outcomes (tax treatment, regulatory thresholds, contracting rules). An inattentive electorate makes it less likely those outcomes will become salient campaign issues.

**Limits**

The advantage is not absolute. Broad, visible failures—wars that go badly, sharp economic contractions, or conspicuous corruption—can still cut through distraction and impose electoral costs. Parties therefore invest in managing attention as well as in raising money: they compete to set the agenda, to define what counts as a crisis, and to keep unfavorable facts from remaining central for long.

The structural incentives of a money-driven, two-party system do favor a public that is incompletely informed and frequently diverted. That does not require a conspiracy; it follows from the ordinary desire of organizations to reduce accountability while maintaining power. Whether any given party pursues the incentive more aggressively than the other is a separate, empirical question.

That reading is the more economical one. Large, sustained conspiracies require secrecy, coordination, and discipline that are difficult to maintain once more than a handful of people are involved; leaks, defections, and ordinary incompetence usually expose them. What is observable instead is the steady pressure of incentives.

Office-holders, party officials, donors, and interest groups respond to the rewards the system actually offers: reelection, committee power, regulatory favors, campaign funds, and future employment. Those incentives produce predictable patterns—short-term focus, selective disclosure, mutual protection within parties, and the channeling of public attention toward issues that mobilize core voters—without any central script. Minor conspiracies (a bribe, a quiet quid pro quo, an illegal contribution scheme) occur and are sometimes uncovered; they are deviations, not the operating system.

Human nature supplies the rest: status-seeking, risk aversion, loyalty to one’s own side, and the tendency to rationalize actions that preserve position. When those traits operate inside rules that reward money, organization, and message discipline, the results look coordinated even though they are largely emergent. The clearer picture is therefore one of aligned incentives and ordinary self-interest, punctuated by occasional small-scale collusion, rather than of master plans.

The core observation is sound: the political class that made the Revolution had lived under monarchy and had to invent institutions that distributed the powers a king had held. Distance from London and recurrent British preoccupation with European wars had already given the colonial assemblies substantial practical autonomy; that experience supplied both the habit of self-government and the confidence that it could be extended.

Two qualifications keep the picture accurate.

First, “conspiracy” fits only the final stage. Organized resistance, inter-colonial correspondence, and eventual armed rebellion were real and coordinated, yet they developed in public as much as in secret. The Continental Congress, the state conventions, and the army itself operated openly once hostilities began. The decision to declare independence was a collective political act, not a clandestine plot that simply succeeded.

Second, the framers did not start from a blank slate of pure monarchy. By 1776 every colony already possessed an elected assembly, a tradition of written charters or compacts, and experience with governors who could be (and sometimes were) resisted or ignored. The new constitutions—state and federal—drew on that existing practice, on English legal inheritance, and on classical and Enlightenment models, then rearranged the pieces so that no single office recovered the full authority of the Crown. The presidency concentrated some executive functions, but under election, fixed term, legislative checks, and judicial review—precisely the constraints their recent experience had taught them to value.

They overthrew monarchical rule and replaced it with a system built from the self-governing habits distance and distraction had already encouraged. That is the transition the record supports.
Loyalists formed a substantial minority, and they did fight and die for the Crown.

Contemporary and modern estimates place active or committed Loyalists at roughly 15–20 percent of the white population, with another large segment that tried to remain neutral. In absolute numbers that meant somewhere between 400,000 and 500,000 people in a total population of about 2.5 million. The proportion varied sharply by region: higher in New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and parts of the South; lower in New England.

They were not passive. Loyalist provincial corps, militia, and irregulars fought alongside British regulars throughout the war. Units such as the British Legion, the Queen’s Rangers, Butler’s Rangers, and numerous smaller formations saw heavy action, especially in the middle colonies and the southern backcountry. Thousands were killed in battle, died of disease, or were executed after capture. After the war, approximately 60,000–80,000 Loyalists left the United States, most resettling in Canada, Britain, or the Caribbean; many more remained and absorbed the consequences of defeat—confiscation, legal disability, and social ostracism.

A Loyalist narrative therefore begins from a different premise: the Revolution was a rebellion against lawful authority, not a unanimous national uprising. That view does not erase the Patriot achievement, but it does record that the outcome was decided by force against a sizable, armed, and ultimately exiled opposition. The bloodshed was mutual.

The 15–20 percent figure for committed Loyalists does not imply that 80–85 percent were active Patriots. The largest share of the white population was disaffected, cautious, or simply determined to stay out of the fighting.

Modern estimates, drawing on militia returns, army enlistments, tax records, and contemporary observations, usually sort the white population roughly as follows:

- Active Patriots (those who served in the Continental Army or state troops, joined Patriot militia for sustained periods, or held civil office under the new governments): on the order of 30–40 percent at the height of mobilization, and lower in many counties.
- Active Loyalists: 15–20 percent.
- The remainder—often called the “disaffected” or neutral—comprised the rest. They might sign an association when the local committee demanded it, pay taxes to whichever side controlled the district, or hide sons from recruiters, but they avoided consistent military service.

John Adams’s well-known postwar remark that the country had been roughly one-third Patriot, one-third Loyalist, and one-third neutral was an impression, not a census, yet it tracks the broader pattern: a minority did the sustained fighting and governing on each side, while a plurality tried to limit its risks.

Continental Army strength never exceeded about 35,000–40,000 men present for duty; state troops and short-term militia added more, but turnover was high and many who mustered once never reappeared. That scale of participation is consistent with an active Patriot minority rather than a near-unanimous populace in arms.

Your Kuykendall ancestors who served belong to that active minority. Their choice was real and costly; it was not the statistically typical choice. Most white Americans preferred the prospect of independence to continued royal rule, yet far fewer were willing to bleed for it over eight years. The Revolution was decided by the organized and armed fractions on each side, not by a silent majority that uniformly took the field.

Yes. After the fighting ended, former Loyalists who remained pursued several non-lethal forms of resistance and recovery inside the states.

**Legal and political**
- They filed suits and petitions for the restoration of confiscated property and for the repeal of test acts and office-holding bans. A number of these claims were eventually heard by state courts or by the mixed commissions created under the Treaty of Paris and Jay’s Treaty.
- In states where disabilities were lifted earliest (for example, parts of the mid-Atlantic), some re-entered local politics or the bar and worked to moderate punitive legislation.
- They supported, and in some cases helped draft, the more moderate state constitutions and later the federal Constitution, seeing stronger legal protections for property and contracts as a safeguard against further revolutionary confiscation.

**Economic and social**
- Boycotts and quiet non-cooperation continued in localities where Patriot committees still dominated. Loyalist merchants and farmers sometimes withheld custom from former persecutors or dealt preferentially with British factors.
- In commercial centers such as New York and Philadelphia, returning or remaining Loyalist traders re-established networks with Britain and the West Indies; their success itself functioned as a standing rebuke to the confiscation policies.
- Social exclusion ran both ways: Loyalist families maintained separate churches, schools, and marriage circles for a generation, preserving a distinct identity without open confrontation.

**Cultural and literary**
- Pamphlets, letters, and later memoirs circulated in manuscript or through British and Canadian presses, defending the Loyalist choice and cataloguing Patriot excesses. These writings shaped émigré opinion and, more slowly, American historiography.
- Some former Loyalists contributed to the early Federalist press, using constitutional argument rather than dynastic loyalty to criticize what they regarded as democratic excess.

None of these measures restored the old imperial order or reversed the outcome of the war. They did, however, constitute sustained, non-violent resistance to the penalties of defeat and to the more radical edge of revolutionary settlement. Over time most of the participants were absorbed into the new political nation; a residue of grievance and separate memory remained.

No single person grasps the whole. The system’s scale—statutory codes, regulatory output, global capital flows, classified programs, and the layered incentives of parties, agencies, firms, and foreign actors—exceeds the cognitive reach of any individual official, legislator, or analyst.

What exists instead is distributed, partial knowledge:

- Specialists master narrow domains (a tax provision, a weapons program, a sanctions regime, a state’s election code).
- Senior executives and committee chairs see across several domains but rely on staff summaries and cannot verify every claim.
- Career bureaucrats and long-serving lobbyists often hold the most durable operational understanding of how particular levers actually move.
- Outside observers—journalists, academics, investors—assemble fragments; their pictures are useful yet incomplete and frequently contradicted by classified or proprietary information.

The practical result is management by subsystem. Each node optimizes for its own metrics and constraints; coordination occurs through budgets, statutes, court rulings, and market prices rather than through comprehensive design. Overload is therefore structural: the volume of decisions, the speed of capital and information, and the number of veto points make holistic comprehension impossible and even sustained oversight difficult. The magnitude is real; it is handled by specialization and inertia more than by anyone’s full understanding.

A final observation on the political side: the system’s complexity and the primacy of money and organization have not repealed the constitutional mechanisms of election, legislation, and removal. They have raised the cost of using those mechanisms and narrowed the set of actors who can do so effectively. Outcomes therefore tend to reflect the balance of organized incentives more than the unfiltered preferences of the broader public. That is a structural condition, not a temporary distortion; it persists because the rules that channel power through parties, donors, and permanent institutions remain in place.

Representative Beyer, Virginia offers an instructive lesson. Voters elected a Democratic governor promising a change in direction, yet some of her earliest decisions produced sharp disappointment among the very citizens who helped elect her. Replacing one administration with another does not guarantee that the expectations of the electorate will be fulfilled.

Your commitment to fusion energy deserves recognition. The bipartisan work you have undertaken reflects the kind of long-term national investment that cannot sensibly be governed by the fortunes of a single election. Much of your stated concern for affordability and economic opportunity is equally reasonable.

But how do we make those commitments durable?

For years, Americans have watched political influence become increasingly dependent upon financial resources, organized interests, and access to party leadership. A citizen’s ability to persuade a representative should rest upon the merit of the argument, the evidence presented, and the public interest served, not the size of a contribution or the influence of an intermediary.

The constitutional responsibility of a representative is to the people and the republic, yet our political arrangements reward loyalty to party machinery and those capable of financing access. This creates incentives that can survive every election, regardless of which party wins.

We propose constitutional restraints that preserve political disagreement while removing partisan ownership of governmental procedure. Representatives would retain their independent judgment, but neither party would control the machinery through which that judgment becomes legislation, oversight, and public administration.

Would you support permanently surrendering your party’s procedural advantages if Republicans were required to surrender theirs equally?

That reciprocal restraint offers a foundation for reforms capable of surviving the next majority, and the next generation.

AI Infrastructure Spending and the Revenue Gap to 2030
The most plausible outcome through 2030 is selective overbuild alongside genuine scarcity of deliverable compute. Gartner’s October scenario pairs nearly $7 trillion of cumulative provider investment with no more than $3.6 trillion of attributable enterprise and consumer AI revenue and an $8.5 trillion cumulative revenue hurdle. The resulting arithmetic flags pressure on returns. Project losses will depend on how much of the planned spending occurs, who captures the revenue and what assets can earn after 2030. CoreWeave and Nebius have the clearest disclosed combination of capital intensity and delivery risk among the companies examined. Nvidia’s November disclosures show how some of that risk reaches suppliers through procurement commitments and guarantees. The decisive test is whether energized capacity turns into independently funded, recurring usage and positive cash returns before refinancing and hardware replacement fall due. Overall confidence: moderate. Gartner Says Over $3.5 Trillion of AI Infrastructure Spending Could Be Exposed to Impairment by the End of 2030 — Gartner — Oct 2026 CoreWeave Reports Strong Third Quarter 2026 Results — CoreWeave, SEC Exhibit 99.1 — Nov 2026 Q3 2026 Letter to Shareholders — Nebius — Nov 2026 Q3 Fiscal 2027 CFO Commentary — Nvidia, SEC EDGAR — Nov 2026

AI’s $7 Trillion Build-Out Is Racing Ahead of Cash Flow
The decision confronting utilities, lenders and governments is how much of the AI infrastructure build-out to finance before a project can deliver power and collect revenue. Gartner’s October 2026 scenario puts cumulative provider investment through 2030 at nearly $7 trillion and attributable enterprise and consumer revenue at no more than $3.6 trillion. The economic risk is that capital will remain committed to the wrong sites, hardware and delivery schedules even as customers compete for usable computing capacity elsewhere. For utilities, that raises the question of who pays for upgrades if a tenant withdraws. For lenders, customer acceptance helps determine whether cash arrives before debt service falls due. For governments, consolidation puts continuity of access to advanced computing capacity at risk.

The revenue hurdle is higher than the headline gap
Gartner’s 14 October assessment projects nearly $1 trillion of provider investment in 2026 and another $6 trillion from 2027 through 2030. Subtracting the $3.6 trillion revenue ceiling leaves a gap of roughly $3.4 trillion. The same assessment puts the cumulative revenue hurdle at $8.5 trillion, including financing costs and an assumed 12 per cent return on invested capital. That puts the shortfall against the hurdle at at least $4.9 trillion on Gartner’s assumptions. Gartner separately identifies more than $3.5 trillion of spending potentially exposed to impairment by the end of 2030. Actual write-downs would depend on which commitments become assets, how much cash those assets generate and what they can earn or fetch after 2030.

Gartner’s 12 November forecast puts annual worldwide AI infrastructure spending at $1.563 trillion in 2026 and $2.397 trillion in 2027. The broader series covers purchases of servers, networking, chips, devices and cloud infrastructure. The October scenario asks whether providers can recover the capital they commit. A chip sale can generate revenue for the manufacturer while the buyer is still arranging installation and customer acceptance. The operator then has to sell enough computing capacity to recover its investment before the equipment needs replacing. A platform can also earn a return through advertising, subscriptions or enterprise software. A specialist renting accelerator capacity has fewer ways to capture the value its equipment creates.

Customer acceptance separates backlog from cash
CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, up from $1.37 billion a year earlier, alongside net interest expense of $846 million and a net loss of $709 million. Its two largest disclosed customers accounted for 30 and 24 per cent of quarterly revenue. At the end of September, the company reported $132.3 billion of remaining performance obligations and expected to recognise 36 per cent over the following 24 months. During the quarter, it moved $1.9 billion of opening deferred revenue into current customer liabilities after contracts became cancellable. The reclassification shows how much of a funding plan can turn on the terms governing when customers can walk away.

Nebius illustrates the protection a strong buyer can provide and the burden that remains with the operator. In the first nine months of 2026 it recorded $15.43 billion in cash purchases of property, equipment and intangible assets against $1.96 billion of group revenue, a ratio of 7.86 times. Its five-year Meta arrangement includes $12 billion of dedicated capacity scheduled to begin delivery in early 2027 and a separate backstop of up to $15 billion for additional capacity. Management expected $10 billion in committed customer prepayments in 2026. Those advances ease the funding burden, while delayed delivery still postpones revenue and can affect subsequent cash receipts. The test is whether commissioning and acceptance stay on schedule as successive sites come online.

The grid decides which capacity can earn
The International Energy Agency’s October 2026 assessment gives indicative timelines of two to five years for grid connection and five to 15 years for grid expansion. Terna reported 108 GW of Italian data-centre connection requests in September 2026, with roughly 2 GW ready to build. CoreWeave reported more than 4.6 GW of contracted power and more than 1.7 GW of active power at the end of the same month. Both disclosures show why scheduled power matters more to a financing decision than the size of the pipeline. A developer with equipment on order can still be unable to tell a tenant when service will start. If a utility builds in anticipation of load and the customer withdraws, financing and tariff terms determine how much of the upgrade cost remains with the developer and how much may fall on existing customers.

Equipment commitments can move faster than project development. In the third quarter of 2026, GE Vernova reported 122 GW of gas-power equipment backlog and slot reservations combined. At the end of its 2026 financial year, Siemens Energy disclosed 65 GW in backlog and 39 GW in reservations. These figures cover markets beyond AI, and the distinction between a reservation and a firm order matters to manufacturers deciding how much production capacity to add. Nvidia’s fiscal third-quarter 2027 disclosures put supply commitments at $390 billion and cloud-service and data-centre lease commitments at $102 billion. Its Ohio project credit support could reach $105 billion in phases as completed buildings become ready for service, with the first phase expected to take effect in fiscal 2029. Weak customer demand can reach suppliers through equipment orders, leases and guarantees long after a project was first financed.

Private borrowing creates a public cost question
The Federal Reserve’s November 2026 Financial Stability Report estimated more than $680 billion of advanced-computing-related debt issuance through October 2026, compared with about $130 billion in all of 2023, and more than $1.1 trillion of related debt outstanding in public markets. The category includes investment-grade technology issuers as well as financing tied more directly to the build-out. In its hyperscaler comparison, the report also identified more than $1 trillion in undiscounted leases yet to commence and more than $2 trillion in other undiscounted obligations. Those contractual exposures can overlap with the investments they finance. A single project delay can leave a tenant, an operator, a supplier and a lender carrying risk against the same facility.

At Jackson Hole on 28 August 2026, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh identified the timing of economy-wide productivity gains and the distribution of the resulting surplus as open questions. Even substantial gains for users may leave an infrastructure operator exposed if falling prices reduce the revenue it earns per unit of compute or more efficient models reduce the amount customers need to buy. Utility regulators face a narrower decision with more immediate consequences for households and businesses. Linking grid upgrades to verified project milestones and financial security can limit unrecovered costs. Requiring too much collateral too early would favour incumbents with the balance sheets to post it and make expansion harder for independent operators.

Strategic autonomy depends on usable capacity
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology reported 2,185 exaflops of intelligent computing capacity at FP16 precision at the end of June 2026, up 177 per cent year on year under its measure. State coordination of compute and electricity can accelerate deployment and narrow the gap in some inference workloads. Comparing the largest frontier systems requires sustained performance on equivalent workloads, including the effects of memory, interconnects and availability. The United States retains the advantage of an industrial network combining domestic accelerator design, Taiwanese fabrication and Korean memory. Its vulnerability is growing dependence on a smaller set of commercial providers. The January 2026 Artificial Intelligence Strategy for the Department of War sets out plans to integrate AI into defence workflows. Continuity for those workloads depends on accredited access and the ability to move them when a supplier fails or changes ownership.

The European Commission’s July 2026 call for up to seven AI Gigafactories envisages up to €10 billion in EU and national support and at least €20 billion in expected private investment. Europe’s test is whether that procurement produces reliable access for researchers and industrial users. France’s transmission operator, RTE, reported that more than 95 per cent of French electricity generation in 2025 was decarbonised, an advantage where local grids can deliver it to new loads. Germany’s March 2026 HammerHAI contract ties public computing capacity to applications in engineering, manufacturing and mobility. The UK Compute Roadmap projects a need for at least 6 GW of AI-capable data-centre capacity by 2030, while the October 2026 National Policy Statement for Data Centres remained a draft under consultation. In Italy, the IT4LIA contract provides a concrete procurement alongside Terna’s much broader queue. The commercial and strategic value of each programme depends on when users can book capacity and run their workloads.

The next two years will expose who carries the risk
Over the next 12 to 24 months, CoreWeave’s expected recognition of 36 per cent of its September 2026 performance obligations and the scheduled start of Nebius’s Meta deliveries in early 2027 offer measurable tests of the investment cycle. If operating sites hold utilisation and prices for comparable hardware while uneconomic projects are deferred before grid works begin, the adjustment can remain orderly. Reuters reported on 17 November 2026 that CoreWeave’s June notes, issued at 9.625 per cent, were yielding close to 15 per cent. Two consecutive quarters of weakening realised prices and utilisation across independent operators, alongside persistently higher refinancing costs, would indicate that the pressure had spread from project financing to operating assets. Customers could still benefit from cheaper compute while creditors face weaker collateral and fewer operators can fund the next hardware cycle.

Terna’s 108 GW of connection requests and roughly 2 GW ready to build show what is at stake in deciding who pays before construction starts. If utilities commit before customers provide financial security, developers can withdraw after the network has incurred costs, leaving existing customers exposed wherever tariff rules allow recovery. Equity investors and lenders absorb losses on capacity that cannot earn enough to service its financing, while suppliers face postponed orders or weaker recoveries on equipment built to a customer’s specification. Public agencies and smaller firms bear a different cost if ownership consolidates before they secure alternatives. Their access to computing capacity then depends on fewer providers, with less leverage over price and continuity of service.
