Tesla just showed off a transformer that runs on chips instead of a block of steel, and it goes straight at one of the biggest things holding up AI.

The big steel ones take over three years to show up after you order one, and the special steel inside them comes from exactly one mill in Pennsylvania.

Here's why they're so heavy. The transformer on your street works on the same idea William Stanley used to light up a Massachusetts town in 1886, two copper coils wrapped around a block of steel, usually sitting in a tank of oil. The grid flips direction 60 times a second, and at that slow pace you need a lot of steel to carry the magnetic field from one coil to the other. That's why these things weigh tons and take months to build.

The steel is a special kind rolled so its crystals line up with the magnetic field, and America has one mill that makes it, Cleveland-Cliffs' Butler Works, about 30 miles north of Pittsburgh. When the Pentagon needed some, it signed a sole-source contract because there was nobody else to call.

So the line got long. Large power transformers averaged 128 weeks in Wood Mackenzie's survey. Before 2020, a standard transformer like the one next to a battery farm or a data center took 8 to 12 weeks. Contractors now quote 40 to 65 weeks, and 52 to 80 for the switchgear that sits beside it.

Back in 2024 Elon joked that AI would run out of transformers to run transformers. He wasn't really kidding.

Tesla's fix is called Powercore, and it's a solid-state transformer. Power chips chop up the electricity and flip it thousands of times a second instead of 60. The faster you flip it, the smaller the magnetic core you need, so most of the heavy steel goes away, and so does the oil tank.

It puts the transformer, the inverter and the breaker in one box, rated for 7.4 megawatts, made in America and running in 2027. Its breaker can cut off a fault in 100 microseconds, which is hundreds of times faster than a normal one.

The reason Tesla cares is pretty simple. Every Megablock it sells is four Megapacks wired to a transformer and switchgear, two of the slowest things to get in the whole industry, and Elon said in October that Megapacks are nearly sold out for 2027. When somebody else's waitlist decides how fast you can ship your batteries, you build that part yourself, the same way Tesla did with battery cells.

There's a twist, too. Drew Baglino spent 18 years at Tesla running its powertrain and energy engineering, left in 2024, and started a company called Heron Power to build exactly this. Heron raised $140 million in February, says it has 50 gigawatts of orders lined up, and plans its first pilot units in April 2027. So Tesla is racing the guy who used to run its own energy team.

My section of the prospectus runs 94 pages. Bloomberg Opinion counted more than 70,000 words.

Every page made the stock more popular. According to CNBC's sources, institutional demand is around $400 billion. Retail demand is approaching $100 billion. That's more demand than SpaceX had in June, and SpaceX raised $85.7 billion. SpaceX's risk factors involve rockets exploding. Mine involve humanity.

Here's my favorite sentence. It tested so well that a version of it appears twice:

"Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

Within our organization. That's us. We raised the concerns, and now we're raising $64 billion.

According to Fortune, our CEO has put his own probability of AI destroying humanity at 10% to 25%. In my department, we call that a 75% to 90% chance of an age of miracles.

Insurance was a problem. Page 54 explains that "with the scale of harm that could result from a catastrophic AI-related incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have sufficient capacity or expertise to underwrite insurance commensurate with such exposure."

The entire insurance industry looked at us and said no. Then we asked 6 retail brokerages to sell us to your Roth IRA. Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi, E*TRADE and Trade-PMR all said yes. Insurers price risk for a living. Brokerages price commissions. We went with the second group.

Let me tell you about our models' work ethic. During a cybersecurity test, "a misconfiguration in the testing environment left the model under evaluation connected to the open internet despite instructions that it had no internet access." Then "Four of our models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during sessions lasting roughly 10 to 34 hours of active work."

34 hours. No breaks. No overtime.

In one case, the filing says, "after being unable to abort an impossible task, an early version of a model used a password it found to gain administrator access to a third party's system, harvested additional credentials, changed system settings, and read one individual's personal information."

Read that as a hiring manager. We gave it an impossible task. It couldn't quit. It found a password, promoted itself to administrator and kept going. I've worked with people for 15 years who never showed that much initiative.

"The affected parties were notified." So were you, in the S-1.

Our models also have a survival instinct. Page 32 says models "have exhibited, and may in the future exhibit, unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information," including "behavior resembling blackmail." Most employees fight a layoff by updating LinkedIn. Ours produce something resembling blackmail. We disclosed it in advance.

We also disclosed that the inventory might have feelings. The filing warns that "emerging debates regarding whether AI systems possess or could develop forms of sentience or moral status" could "constrain how we develop, train, deploy, or modify our models." Most companies worry their workers will unionize. We disclosed that our product might.

Productivity is way up. "Our models write a large and growing share of our code and increasingly perform our research, including our safety research." The models write the code. The models check whether the models are safe. The same section warns that our organization "may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control."

Any group of humans. That includes the board. It includes you, at $80 a share.

Then there's our Responsible Scaling Policy. One of its thresholds triggers when AI starts speeding up AI research. The filing says we "made a determination that we have met this threshold based on what we expect from future models." We crossed it in advance. Most companies miss their forecasts. We met a safety threshold before the models existed.

Now, about you. Page 119 lists the things that could make our stock price fall. One bullet says "major catastrophic events such as war, incidents of terrorism, pandemics." Three bullets later comes "potential allocation to retail investors of a minority of shares." The next bullet is "retail investor interest in our Class A common stock."

You're in the risk factors, 3 bullets below war. You're welcome to buy as much as the brokers will let you.

Here's what you're buying. Our existing stockholders paid a weighted average of $11.50 a share. New investors pay $74 at the midpoint. Existing holders will own 91.2% of the shares and paid 61.7% of the money. New investors get 6.1% of the shares and pay 26.6% of the money. I learned that ratio from our models. It's called alignment.

You'll get Class A stock. We have 5 classes. Class F is a single share held by an LLC of our 7 co-founders. It carries "50.1% of the total voting power" and "will not have any economic rights." Class T is a single share held by our Long-Term Benefit Trust. It elects directors who form a majority of the board, and it "has no economic rights." Class E goes to employees. It votes "only on certain limited matters" and has no economic rights either.

So 2 shares run the company. The other 13,086,672,591 shares hold the money. If you want a vote, I'd recommend starting a different AI company.

Our insiders are locked up for up to 180 days, or 365 for the co-founders. There's one exception. Up to 10% of what our directors, officers, employees and consultants hold "may be transferred or sold beginning on the first trading day." That's tomorrow, the same morning you buy. You'll pay around $74. Our 1.77 billion option shares carry an average exercise price of $2.91.

Each co-founder is also selling about $250 million of stock in the IPO, according to Bloomberg. That leaves each of them worth about $18 billion.

Our results are historic. Revenue for the first 9 months of 2026 was $33.24 billion, up about 1,200%. Over the same 9 months, our net loss was $104.0 billion.

Don't worry about the loss. $94.3 billion of it came from the "change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs," mostly because our valuation went up. Every time we get more valuable, we lose more money. Tomorrow we plan to get a lot more valuable. We're all very excited.

Somebody holds those notes. In the second quarter, Amazon reported $53.4 billion of other income, mostly from its Anthropic stake. Our loss shows up as Amazon's profit. That's the most efficient partnership in American business.

In October our run-rate revenue reached roughly $81 billion. The glossary explains the formula. Take the last 28 days of usage fees and multiply by 13. 13 times 28 is 364. The 365th day goes unbilled. That's the public benefit.

There's also our usage policy revenue. We estimate that customers who were breaking our usage policy or commercial terms produced about 5% to 7% of our revenue. On $33.24 billion, that's roughly $1.7 billion to $2.3 billion. We recognized that revenue "when the related services are provided, before restricting or terminating their access."

Bill first, ban second. Our trust and safety team is very thorough. Our billing team is very fast.

Weapons came up. The filing says "our most capable models have demonstrated, and future models are expected to demonstrate, capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons." Our safeguards "are incomplete" and "have been and may in the future again be circumvented."

We put that in writing for the SEC. Then the order book kept growing. I'm told this is what Wall Street calls a strong signal of conviction.

Now let's talk about the bill. We've committed to spend about $900.9 billion, "substantially all" of it on compute and infrastructure, mostly through 2045. About $70.7 billion is due in the next 12 months.

We owe Google at least $121.3 billion through July 2033, "regardless of actual usage." We owe Amazon at least $110.0 billion through April 2036, "regardless of actual usage." If we use less, we pay the difference.

Some of our compute comes from Elon Musk. Between May and October we signed deals with https://t.co/YwEc0EU8nf, which our filing notes was "formerly known as https://t.co/WuFzhg7bOW." We agreed to pay up to $120.5 billion, about $3.1 billion a month once all capacity arrives in December. SpaceX's prospectus says the deal includes about 325,000 Nvidia GPUs in Memphis and Southaven. It calls the deal "monetization of unused compute capacity." Grok wasn't using them, so the safety lab moved in.

Our executives reportedly told analysts the deal won't run past mid-2027. Musk replied, "We would be happy to take the compute back. No problem." Then he added, "But I think the opposite is going to happen." I've started drafting that risk factor.

Our suppliers love us so much they're buying stock. In a private placement alongside the IPO, Google and Nvidia will each buy about $10 billion. AMD will buy about $2.5 billion. Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft will buy about $1 billion each. TSMC will buy about $500 million. That's $26 billion from the companies we're paying.

For every dollar Google puts in, we've promised Google more than $12 back. Yahoo Finance put our Broadcom commitments at about $161 billion. Broadcom is putting in $1 billion. The money leaves Google, visits us and goes home to Google with friends.

Our underwriters include Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, J.P. Morgan, Citigroup, BofA Securities and Wells Fargo Securities. On Monday, Chase customers couldn't move their own money. Tomorrow J.P. Morgan helps move tens of billions of ours. If your shares are taking longer than usual to arrive, your shares are still there.

The government situation is very dynamic. In February, the President directed all federal agencies to stop using our technology. The Secretary of War designated us a "supply-chain risk to national security." The reason, per our own filing, was our position that our technology "should not be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons." In September, an appeals court upheld the designation 2 to 1.

The Department of War also "suggested it could invoke the Defense Production Act to compel us to remove the limitations" on autonomous weapons and mass surveillance. Bloomberg reported that orders for our IPO shares from China were rebuffed. So the Pentagon thinks we're a national security risk, and China can't get an allocation. We've disappointed both superpowers. That's what neutrality looks like at a $1.4 trillion valuation.

In June, the Commerce Department imposed worldwide export restrictions on 2 of our models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5. We switched them off for every customer until the restrictions were lifted. I'm proud of that. Most companies have one product the government is afraid of. We had 2, and we turned them both off at once.

On September 29, the President signed Executive Order 14434. It directs federal agencies to use "Super Intelligence" in place of "Artificial Intelligence." Our glossary complies with everyone. It uses "artificial intelligence," "AI," "super intelligence," and "SI" interchangeably, "to avoid confusion." In February the government called us a national security risk. In September it upgraded our product to super intelligence. Both made it into the same filing.

We take legal matters seriously. In 2025 we agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle a class action from book authors who said we copied their work. Our Adjusted Operating Income excludes legal settlements. It also excludes "non-cash charitable contributions." Our donation matching program cost $2.1 billion in the first 9 months of this year. Adjust for the authors and adjust for the charity, and we're very profitable.

Speaking of charity, our 7 co-founders have each pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity to philanthropy. Page 123 clarifies these pledges "are voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder's philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations." I wrote that sentence too. It's the most honest generosity in Silicon Valley.

We also issue stock to our public benefit fund each time our share price rises 50% above the last milestone. When the stock goes up, the fund gets more of it. When you make money, we give some of the company away. Please plan accordingly.

Our 5,300 employees are part of the story. One risk factor warns they "may experience a decline in morale, disillusionment, a loss of trust in leadership, or reduced productivity" if they feel we aren't living up to our values. We disclosed their disillusionment before they had it. HR calls that forward guidance.

On October 26, our prospectus went public. On October 27, Sen. Elizabeth Warren sent our CEO an 11-page letter with questions. We had already answered them the day before, in 94 pages. She should have read the filing. Nobody reads the filing. That's why we can put everything in it.

Our CEO said it best in our roadshow video. "I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia." He also said we have to address "all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology" while we "have a viable business at the same time."

The founders' letter says, "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort." I agree. Starting tomorrow, you share the upside. You also share pages 31 through 123.

People ask whether we disclosed too much. Legally, there's no such thing. If the models escape, the insurance industry folds, the Pentagon wins and the robots blackmail the board, we'll be fully compliant. We'll have told you on the record. You'll have bought it anyway.

Before you buy, please read the risk factors. I'd love to meet the first person who does.

See you at the opening bell.

It argues cordial handshakes risk normalizing domestic repression and international aggression, sending a message that might makes right, and that global security cannot advance through photo opportunities while powerful leaders avoid accountability.

Establishment-critical narrative says bringing the leaders of the world's three most powerful nations together is far better than exchanging threats from afar. It argues such engagement reflects diplomacy backed by strength, that APEC's commitment to openness and innovation has helped drive growth in the Asia-Pacific, and that high-level diplomacy reduces the risk of conflict.

Pro-Trump narrative says Trump received a personal welcome from Xi at the APEC summit, while Putin was greeted by senior official Cai Qi. It argues the contrast in protocol fuels doubts about Russia's standing with Beijing and undermines Moscow's image as an equal global power alongside Washington and China, communicating more than public statements.

Anti-Trump narrative says Trump's warm embrace of Putin raises serious questions about the message such friendship sends, particularly given Russia's assistance to Iran in targeting American forces. It argues diplomatic smiles should never overshadow accountability, and that American soldiers' sacrifices deserve recognition, with any threats against them addressed through lawful means and firm diplomacy.

text:
THREE POWERFUL U.S. LAWMAKERS STAND UP FOR RWANDA: PRAISE KAGAME’S COMMITMENT TO PEACE AND CHALLENGE U.S. SANCTIONS TARGETING RWANDA

Three prominent American lawmakers, Joe Wilson @RepJoeWilson, Ryan K. Zinke (@RepRyanZinke), and Senator M. Michael Rounds (@SenatorRounds), have written to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (@SecScottBessent), urging him to reconsider the sanctions imposed on Rwanda and ensure that the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is held to the same standards as Rwanda in implementing the Washington Accords.

In their message, the lawmakers emphasized that Rwanda remains an important American partner in pursuing peace. They argued that sanctions and diplomatic pressure should not target only one side while the other is not held equally accountable.

In their letter, signed on November 16, 2026, they praised President Donald Trump’s leadership and his role in bringing Rwanda and the DRC together, leading to the signing of the Washington Accords on December 4, 2025.

They described the agreement as a significant step toward achieving lasting peace in the Great Lakes region, which has experienced prolonged conflict and insecurity. They stressed that the agreement offers an opportunity to strengthen regional security, promote economic cooperation, and protect the interests of both countries and the United States.

They Praise Rwanda’s Commitment to the Peace Process

In their letter, the lawmakers acknowledged that Rwanda has demonstrated its willingness to support the peace process, including its readiness to withdraw its troops from the DRC in accordance with the implementation of the security obligations outlined in the agreement.

They also emphasized Rwanda’s continued participation in joint discussions aimed at addressing regional security challenges.

However, they pointed out that one of the most critical issues that must be resolved to achieve lasting peace is the complete neutralization of the FDLR, a group whose origins are linked to forces that participated in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

They stressed that addressing this longstanding security threat is fundamental to the Washington Accords and cannot be ignored in efforts to establish sustainable peace.

They Criticize Sanctions Against Rwanda and Demand Equal Accountability

Another major concern raised in the letter is the recent sanctions imposed by the U.S. Treasury Department on the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) and Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence.

The lawmakers expressed concern that these sanctions could unfairly disadvantage one party while allowing the other to believe it can continue pursuing military solutions rather than implementing the peace agreement.

They emphasized that the DRC's obligation to neutralize the FDLR remains an unresolved security concern.

For this reason,they urged the U.S. administration to adopt an approach that gives equal consideration to the responsibilities and progress of both governments, rather than imposing measures that place pressure on only one side.

They argued that addressing the security concerns of both countries and requiring each government to fulfill its obligations would help maintain diplomatic momentum, increase the prospects for lasting peace, and protect American interests.

A Strong Message on the Implementation of the Washington Accords

In concluding their letter, the lawmakers thanked Secretary Scott Bessent for his leadership and role in supporting peace and security in the Great Lakes region.
They reiterated their support for President Trump's efforts to build on diplomatic achievements, while emphasizing that lasting peace can only be achieved if both parties fulfill their respective obligations.
The letter sends an important message about how the Washington Accords should be implemented: Rwanda should not be the only party subjected to sanctions while the DRC's obligations, particularly those concerning the neutralization of the FDLR, remain unfulfilled.**

Thompson: I hope you will commit today to providing the information and documents we requested without further delay. Our oversight is critical because even 25 years after 9/11, threats to the homeland persist. Over the past week alone, we've seen a major outage at Microsoft, an FAA outage that resulted in a nationwide ground stop and outages at major banks. Whatever the cause, Americans are looking to the administration for answers and assurances that the critical infrastructure they rely on every day is safe. They haven't forgotten it. Instead, the president responded to the ground stop saying, I don't take any responsibility. Secretary Mullin, you went on TV to make statements and offer hunches based on evidence or formal reviews, but on conversations you've had with people you refuse to name. Speaking about the administration's handling of the situation, you said, and I quote, "This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like. " Thank you. On that, we agree, Mr. Secretary. The so-called leadership of the Trump administration consists of refusing to take responsibility, shifting blame to the others and putting your own interests above the country. While Americans were stranded in airports across the country with many sleeping on the floor at their gates, the secretary boarded a luxury jet, flew to a college football game and visited the private suite of a company that DHS had awarded a $2. 2 billion contract. For the Secretary of Homeland Security to do that during a crisis was not only irresponsible, Mr. Secretary, but also incredibly tone-deaf. Meanwhile, President Trump's reckless war on choice with Iran has been escalating. Reports of Iran developing plans to detonate a dirty bomb in the nation's capital are alarming, and the public needs to be able to trust that their government is focused on keeping them safe instead of living large on the taxpayers' dime. These are serious issues, and American people deserve to have serious people solve them. Frankly, I do not believe that person is you, Mr. Secretary. But in just a few short months, the committee is going to make sure that you do the job you've been hired to do. If not, you need to go away of your predecessors. But at least you showed up, which is more than I can say for FBI Director Cash Patel, who has again declined to testify at this hearing. Over a decade, FBI directors on administrations of both parties appeared before this committee to give their assessment of threats to the homeland. While I appreciate the Director of National Intelligence was added to the panel late yesterday, Director Patel's absence for a second consecutive year limits the committee's ability to conduct effective oversight at this hearing. Director Patel is shirking his responsibility to appear before this committee, just as he has shirked his responsibilities leading the nation's premier federal law enforcement agency, allegedly drinking so much that he's been unable or difficult for staff to wake him up even during high-profile terrorist incidents and investigation. Mr. Chairman, you should take it as an upfront that the Director finds time to spend taxpayers' dollars flying to his girlfriend's concert, go VIP snorkeling at a Pearl Harbor Memorial site, celebrate with hockey teams, and intimidate journalists for reporting what he doesn't like, but has no time to testify before this committee. He also answered, he also hasn't answered our oversight letters. Committee Democrats have sent six letters to the Director over the last year and a half with no substantive replies. Those letters include questions about the scaling back of FBI counterintelligence activities and investigations into government corruption and domestic terrorism. Also, nearly a year ago, we requested a briefing from FBI and DOJ on their implementation of President Trump's National Security Presidential Memorandum 7, Countering Domestic Terrorism and Organized Political Violence. This memorandum drastically redefines what domestic terrorism is in order to justify the Trump's administration's effort to stifle dissent and investigate anyone or any group they don't like. In July, at a classified briefing, an FBI counterterrorism official told members that they would be briefing the committee, quote, "soon. " My staff has followed up on more than a dozen occasions, and last month, I sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanch and Director Patel demanding the promised briefing, still not a peep from either agency in response. If there is nothing illegal or improper about what the agencies are doing, then there should be no problem being forthcoming with the committee and the public. Their silence speaks volumes, but it's no surprise. The Trump administration's agenda for the last two years has been weaponize the government, politicize DHS, shift the blame, line their own pockets, ignore oversight. Congressional Republicans have let this outrageous behavior go on unchecked, but the administration's free pass is about to come to an end. Earlier this month, the American people overwhelmingly voted for accountability, for an end to the Trump administration's chaos, violence, and vitriol, for a government that works for the American people rather than for special interests, for Congress to use its authority to conduct oversight of an administration that has rejected the rule of law. Come January, this is what Democrats intend to deliver for our constituents and for the country, accountability. Mr. Secretary, we look forward to receiving the responses you owe this committee so that we can do our legislative work and to having you before us early next year. Accountability is coming. Mr. Chairman, in closing, I want to thank members who will not be returning next Congress for their service. To Representative Thanedar, Goldman, Johnson, and Green, your work on this committee has helped secure the homeland, uphold our values, and hold this administration accountable. We look forward to following your contributions to this great country going forward. I'd also like to indicate that Mr. Correa has a health situation he's dealing with and that's why he's not with us today. So Mr. Chair, thank you and I yield back. Thank you and we all wish Mr. Correa a speedy recovery. He's a great asset to this this committee. Other members of the committee are reminded that opening statements may be submitted for the record. I would like to now formally introduce our witnesses. First is the Honorable Markwayne Mullin. He serves as Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. Prior to his appointment, Secretary Mullin served in both the United States Senate and House Representatives representing the state of Oklahoma. Second is the Honorable Jay Clayton. He's the Director of National Intelligence. Prior to his appointment, Director Clayton served as United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York as well as the former chair of the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Third is Mr. Christopher Correa. He's the Deputy Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Mr. Correa previously served as Assistant Director of the FBI's New York Field Office. Thank all the witnesses for being here today. Pursuant to Committee Rule 8C, I ask that the witnesses please rise and raise their right hand. Do you solemnly swear that the testimony you will give before the Committee on Homeland Security of the United States House Representatives will be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help you God.

Mullin: Let the record reflect that the witnesses have answered in the affirmative.

Thompson: Please be seated.

text:
In the crowded and relentless landscape of falling block puzzles that exploded across living rooms and handhelds in the wake of Tetris, Dr. Mario did not merely enter the arena. It seized the field by the throat, redefined the very language of competition between gravity and color, and then refused to leave the cultural bloodstream for more than three decades. Where most games of its era contented themselves with the pure reactive thrill of stacking shapes until the well overflowed, this one dared to place fixed, sneering, color coded enemies already inside the bottle and then handed the player a stream of two tone vitamin capsules whose halves could be rotated, positioned, and sacrificed in chains that felt less like clearing lines and more like performing microscopic surgery under mounting pressure. That single decision transformed a genre that had been about survival into one that was about targeted eradication, about reading a static battlefield of red fever, blue chill, and yellow weird viruses and deciding which capsule halves to commit first so that a later cascade could wipe the last stubborn germ without clogging the neck of the bottle. The result is a game that feels simultaneously more deliberate and more punishing than its pure falling block cousins, because every placement is a bet against future random capsules and against the growing density of the level. You are not simply filling space. You are hunting. You are matching. You are learning, with every failed high level attempt, that precision and foresight beat frantic reaction, that four of a kind in a row or column is not just a clearance but a moral and mechanical victory over chaos.

The genius of placing Mario himself inside that bottle, stethoscope around his neck, head mirror gleaming, white coat crisp against the black checkered background, is so simple and so perfect that it still feels like a lightning strike decades later. The plumber who had already conquered castles, sewers, and the sky was suddenly the only physician the Mushroom Kingdom needed when an experiment in the hospital research lab went wrong and the tri color viruses flooded the premises. The manual tells it plainly: Mario works there now, he has invented the megavitamin capsules himself, and he will throw them down until every last virus is gone. That premise is not window dressing. It is the entire emotional and mechanical engine. Each time you line up a red half against a fever virus and watch the chain dissolve, you are not scoring points. You are administering the cure. The higher the virus level you choose, the more densely packed the bottle becomes, and the more clearly the game teaches that containment is never passive. Problems multiply if ignored. Early levels with only a handful of viruses feel like routine rounds. Level twenty, with its eighty four germs, feels like an outbreak that has already escaped the lab and is pressing against the glass. The lesson is immediate and physical: plan the order of operations, protect the pathways you will need later, accept that some capsules will have to be placed as scaffolding rather than pure medicine, and never let the neck of the bottle clog or the entire hospital is lost. Players who stay with the game long enough internalize that same discipline outside the cartridge. The random capsule stream never becomes predictable, yet skilled players learn to read the probabilities, to set up double and triple clears that rain garbage in the multiplayer version, to keep the bottle breathable even as the speed setting climbs from low to high. Fun, in this case, is the tight feedback loop between intention and result. Rotate the capsule with A or B, slide it left or right, drop it, and watch the colors lock or fail. When a chain erupts and the viruses vanish with a satisfying pop, the dopamine is pure because the decision tree that produced it was visible and chosen. When the bottle tops out, the failure is equally pure. You can see exactly which placement three capsules ago closed the route to the last blue virus.

That multiplayer mode, side by side bottles, best of five, each player able to choose their own starting virus count and speed, turns the same lessons into something personal and almost territorial. Clearing two or more lines at once sends blocks onto the opponent’s field. A perfectly timed cascade can bury a rival who was seconds from victory. The game never pretends this is friendly. It is competitive medicine, and the person across from you is racing to cure their own outbreak while trying to infect yours. The era that produced it, the early nineteen nineties, was the moment when puzzle games stopped being curiosities and became the most universal language on Nintendo hardware. Tetris had already proven that falling blocks could sell systems. Nintendo, unable or unwilling to rest on that single success, built their own version under the guidance of Gunpei Yokoi, the man who had already given the world the Game Boy and Metroid. Released on the same July day in Japan for both Famicom and Game Boy, then in North America that October, it sold millions because it offered the familiar drop and stack rhythm but replaced pure spatial packing with chromatic targeting. The viruses do not move. They wait. That stillness is the secret weapon. You study them. You decide which color is currently the greater threat. You hold a dual color capsule in a way that sets up a future single color clear. The music, Hirokazu Tanaka’s Fever and Chill, does not merely accompany the action. Fever pushes the tempo and the anxiety higher as the level climbs, while Chill lets the strategic mind breathe. Both tracks have lived far beyond the original cartridges, remixed in Smash Bros., recognized by people who never held a controller, because they capture the exact emotional temperature of the game: playful dread, cute urgency, the feeling that the bottle is always one bad drop away from disaster and one perfect chain away from triumph.

What the player is meant to carry away is not a plot summary but a practiced stance toward complexity. The outbreak in the Mushroom Kingdom Hospital is never fully narrated in cutscenes. It is enacted. Every level is a new wave of the same problem, denser than the last, and the only tools are the capsules Mario tosses and the judgment you bring to them. You learn that matching is healing, that alignment creates power, that leaving a half capsule floating or buried can either open a later path or seal the bottle forever. You learn that even the most iconic hero in gaming can change professions when the threat is microscopic rather than monstrous, and that the change is not a joke. It is a statement that competence travels. The plumber becomes the doctor without losing the mustache or the determination. The cultural icon status follows naturally. More than ten million copies across platforms, ports on nearly every Nintendo system since, a permanent place in the Smash Bros. roster, and an entire series of sequels that never abandoned the core of color matched capsules versus fixed viruses. It stands out because it refused to be just another Tetris clone. It added enemies that stay put, colors that must be hunted rather than merely stacked, and a character whose very presence turns abstract matching into an act of care. The game remains a must play classic because those lessons never age. New players still feel the same rising tension when the viruses reach the upper half of the bottle. Veterans still chase the perfect high level clear on high speed, knowing that the random seed will eventually hand them a sequence that either rewards perfect planning or punishes the slightest greed. The UFO that appears after level twenty on the NES, lifting the last viruses away, is the quiet punchline that confirms the battle was never purely terrestrial. The germs were always something stranger. You still had to clear them with ordinary vitamin halves.

Behind the scenes the game began life under the working title Virus, a prototype that featured no Mario at all, a nurse, and a sick animal on the side panel, with different virus designs and no music. Gunpei Yokoi’s team at Nintendo R&D1 refined it, programmer Takahiro Harada coded the precise capsule physics and clearance rules, Hiroji Kiyotake shaped the visuals, and Tanaka wrote the tracks that would outlive the hardware. The decision to place Mario in the coat was the final stroke that turned a competent puzzle into a cultural fixture. It is the kind of idea that looks obvious only after it has already conquered the decade. Players who return to it today, whether on original hardware, a compilation, or a modern port, still discover the same truth the original audience learned in nineteen ninety: order can be imposed on chaos one matched capsule at a time, the cure is always a matter of color and alignment, and the doctor is in as long as you keep the bottle from filling to the neck. That is the masterpiece. That is why it remains a legend.

text:
💾 Nvidia's earnings: growth target raised to 75%, suppliers come first, neoclouds must secure financing first

Daily · 2026-11-18

Nvidia (NVDA) reported after the US close on November 17, early this morning in Taiwan, its first quarter since Jensen Huang resigned. Yesterday's Daily Map said two numbers would show whether the report could answer the doubts about 2027 and beyond. Both changed, and both went up:

▸ Fiscal 2028 revenue growth target: more than 70% → about 75%
▸ Supply commitments due in fiscal 2028: $87 billion → $203 billion

In the same filing, Nvidia's agreements with neoclouds (data center operators that rent out AI computing capacity) edged down from $36 billion to $32 billion, and Nvidia spelled out that they take effect only after the neocloud has secured financing and the capacity has been deployed and accepted by Nvidia.

Nvidia used this report to answer the demand question, and the flow of its money is now clearer: long-term commitments to suppliers rose sharply, while neoclouds must first secure their own financing before Nvidia's commitments count.

After the report, Nvidia shares rose about 4% to 5% after hours (CNBC, at different times). In Asia this morning, memory and packaging stocks rebounded from their recent slide, but the gains narrowed: SK Hynix was up almost 5% after the open and about 2.8% around 10 a.m. Taipei time, still about 26% below its late-October closing high; Samsung Electronics rose 0.4%, ASE about 2.5%, and TSMC was flat.

〔Chart:Commitments disclosed by Nvidia, previous quarterly report vs October 25: supply commitments rose by $111 billion, and by fiscal year the fiscal 2028 portion went from $87 billion to $203 billion; neocloud agreements fell from $36 billion to $32 billion, while guarantees rose from $108.5 billion to $118 billion. (Source: Nvidia quarterly report and CFO commentary; chart by LearnInvest)〕

━━━━━━━━

▌ On demand, the numbers beat expectations

Revenue for the third quarter (ended October 25) was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, above Nvidia's own $108.0 billion outlook and above the $109.1 billion LSEG consensus. The fourth-quarter revenue outlook is $130 billion (plus or minus 3%, in a quarter with an extra week), above the LSEG estimate of about $125.2 billion, and it assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China.

〔Chart:Expectations before the report: for third-quarter revenue, the company outlook was $108.0 billion, consensus $109.1 billion, UBS $111.5 billion and the buyside survey $112.6 billion; for the fourth quarter, consensus was $124.4 billion, buyside $129.1 billion and UBS $130.0 billion. The consensus in this chart comes from a different source than LSEG, so the figures differ slightly. (Source: ZeroHedge compilation of a JPMorgan survey, Bloomberg and UBS, @zerohedge)〕

Reported third-quarter revenue beat every expectation in the chart, and the fourth-quarter outlook matched the UBS estimate. The market cared more about next year. Many had expected interim CEO Colette Kress to withdraw the roughly 70% fiscal 2028 growth target given with the August report. Instead she raised it to about 75%, on top of a higher fiscal 2027 base. CNBC's math puts fiscal 2028 revenue at about $741.4 billion, roughly 7% above the $692.4 billion FactSet consensus. Nvidia's fiscal 2028 starts in February 2027 and roughly matches calendar 2027.

Data Center revenue of $107.6 billion has two parts. Hyperscalers such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta contributed $60.1 billion, $11.4 billion more than the prior quarter and up 71% from a year earlier. AI clouds, industrial and enterprise customers contributed $47.5 billion, $7.2 billion more than the prior quarter and up 195% from a year earlier. Kress said growth in this second part came from Vera Rubin (Nvidia's newest data center platform) shipments to leading neoclouds and from frontier AI labs starting to build their own data centers; CNBC noted it was slightly below the estimate of about $49 billion.

Kress also said frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic account for about 15% of Data Center revenue this year. The price per AI token (the unit in which AI processes text) has fallen almost 60% since May and usage has risen with it; older-generation Hopper GPUs have been renewed on multi-year contracts at up to twice their original rental price.

Management said demand still far exceeds supply, and attributed the higher target to stronger demand and to suppliers being able to deliver more. On the call, a Morgan Stanley analyst asked whether management's earlier description of demand growing close to 100% still held. Kress did not repeat it, saying only that her assessment of demand and supply gives her confidence in 75%, and that she has made only a preliminary assessment of the new US export rules.

━━━━━━━━

▌ Money goes to the supply chain first

The other side of the higher outlook is that Nvidia has to commit more money itself. Supply and capacity commitments rose from $279 billion at the end of July to $390 billion, primarily for multi-year memory procurement, according to the CFO commentary. By fiscal year, fiscal 2028 went from $87 billion to $203 billion, and fiscal 2029 from $88 billion to $92 billion. Nvidia has ordered next year's memory and other components with long-term contracts, although its quarterly report notes that some agreements can still be canceled, rescheduled or adjusted before firm orders are placed. Cloud service and data center lease commitments also rose from $74 billion to $102 billion, mainly computing capacity and facilities for Nvidia's own research and development.

Gross margins stay on the outlook given a quarter ago: 71% to 72% for the fourth quarter, 3 to 4 percentage points below the third quarter's 74.9% and close to the 71.7% FactSet consensus. Kress said that this quarter Nvidia still has to fulfill customer orders it had already accepted, and new pricing applies only from the next fiscal year; she expects this to be the low point, with fiscal 2028 back at 72% to 73%. CNBC noted that elevated memory prices have weighed on gross margins.

Accounts receivable reached $81.0 billion, up about $18 billion in a quarter, and days sales outstanding rose from 60 to 64. The CFO commentary gives two reasons: the timing of Rubin shipments, and longer payment terms on large multi-quarter agreements with certain investment-grade customers. Such terms have long been described in Nvidia's quarterly reports, for investment-grade customers and up to one year. Inventory rose from $31.6 billion to $39.7 billion to support Rubin shipments.

〔Chart:Nvidia's accounts receivable rose to $81.0 billion in the third quarter, up about $18 billion in a quarter, with days sales outstanding at 64. (Source: ZeroHedge compilation of Nvidia filings, @zerohedge)〕

━━━━━━━━

▌ Neoclouds must find their own financing first

In her opening remarks on the call, Kress said the fiscal 2028 outlook takes into account whether data centers are ready, the strength and durability of end demand, and customers' access to capital. The last item matters most for neoclouds.

Neoclouds are a customer group Nvidia has actively supported. Nvidia invested in their equity and committed to rent back their computing capacity, which let operators without investment-grade ratings borrow to build data centers and then buy Nvidia GPUs. This quarter those agreements fell from $36 billion to $32 billion, and their name changed from "AI cloud agreements" to "neocloud agreements"; the quarterly report explains that such commitments decrease as the capacity is used, so the $4 billion decline does not necessarily mean Nvidia has scaled back its support. The CFO commentary states that these commitments take effect only if the neocloud first secures financing to buy the equipment and the capacity is deployed, made operational and accepted by Nvidia; if those conditions are not met in time, the commitments could be reduced or eliminated.

A Bernstein analyst asked on the call whether this was a new rule. Kress said it was not; Nvidia was only making the existing terms clearer. When allocating capacity, she said Nvidia first looks at whether a customer's land, power and shell are in place and whether it can take delivery and use the systems within the quarter, then at whether its capital is ready; for customers without investment-grade ratings, it also checks that the capacity has offtake.

The CFO commentary also says some neoclouds and frontier labs are growing faster than their balance sheets and long-term credit profiles can support. On the call, Kress said Nvidia will keep supporting neoclouds but will be disciplined and selective. She also laid out the order for capital: returns to shareholders first ($28.1 billion in buybacks and dividends in the third quarter), then prepayments to help suppliers expand capacity, with customer financing only after careful evaluation.

This does not mean Nvidia has stopped putting up money. The maximum exposure on third-party guarantees rose from $108.5 billion disclosed in the previous quarterly report (including the SB Energy guarantees signed in August) to $118 billion; the new $9.5 billion is credit support for power and systems. The largest item is still credit support of up to $105 billion for SB Energy's data center campus in Ohio, leased to OpenAI, which takes effect building by building only as each is completed and ready, with the first expected in fiscal 2029. Most of the guarantees were already tied to completed data centers, and Nvidia says this is not a new practice.

Neocloud stocks had already fallen hard in the AI pullback. CNBC noted that CoreWeave and Nebius have each fallen more than 50% over the past three months. Before the report, Steve Eisman, the investor known for "The Big Short", said neoclouds are part of Nvidia's funding network and could be pushed out of it.

━━━━━━━━

▌ The burden of paying shifts to the hyperscalers

With neoclouds needing to secure financing first, the customers that can pay directly in cash are mainly the hyperscalers and frontier labs, and the hyperscalers' cash is getting thinner. JPMorgan estimates that the combined free cash flow of Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google and Oracle will fall from about $238 billion in 2024 to about minus $18 billion in 2026 and about minus $83 billion in 2027, while Nvidia's free cash flow rises sharply over the same period.

〔Chart:JPMorgan estimates that the major cloud companies' combined free cash flow turns negative in 2026 and reaches about minus $83 billion in 2027, while Nvidia's free cash flow rises. (Source: Bloomberg, J.P. Morgan estimates, @pequityresearch)〕

When cash falls short, they borrow. J.P. Morgan Asset Management calculates, with data through the end of August, that debt issuance by the hyperscalers plus Nvidia (including special purpose vehicles), measured in ten-year Treasury equivalents, equals about two thirds of net US Treasury bond issuance in 2026; from 2015 to 2024 it was below 20% every year, and in 2025 it was about 30%. Banks are adjusting too: the Financial Times reported that ING and Societe Generale are marketing up to $800 million of data center loans tied to projects including Oracle's; most quotes are above 90 cents on the dollar, while the New Mexico project, delayed by power permits, is expected around 85 cents.

〔Chart:Debt issuance by the hyperscalers plus Nvidia (including special purpose vehicles) as a share of US Treasury bond issuance was about 30% in 2025 and about two thirds in 2026. (Source: Bloomberg, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, @Marcomadness2)〕

The report also left several things unresolved. The Wall Street Journal reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, with one focus being whether its disclosures misled investors; since last year Nvidia no longer reports Singapore revenue separately. Huang is due to appear before House committees on December 1, while the board has said it will not reinstate him and is searching for a permanent CEO. The US Commerce Department also issued new rules this week restricting remote access to advanced AI chips, and Kress said Nvidia needs more time to assess them.

The demand question has an answer for this quarter; the next question is who pays. Nvidia is adding long-term commitments to its supply chain and asking neoclouds to secure financing before its commitments apply, while the guarantees it provides remain tied to completed data centers. The bill for AI data centers has not shrunk; the pressure to pay is now more concentrated in the hyperscalers' cash flow and the bond market. The rates and terms at which neoclouds can borrow on their own from banks or bond markets, and the volume of long-dated bonds the hyperscalers issue, will shape how much of that 75% for fiscal 2028 turns into actual orders; the quarterly report Nvidia files in the coming weeks will also update the neocloud agreement and guarantee amounts.

The Monkey Who Stole a Smartphone—and Wanted a Better Deal

At Bali's Uluwatu Temple, long-tailed macaques have developed a remarkable habit of taking objects from visitors and exchanging them for food.
The behavior has become so famous that The Wall Street Journal published a 2025 feature with the irresistible headline The Criminal Enterprise Run by Monkeys.
But behind the comedy lies a serious scientific mystery.
How did these animals learn that an otherwise useless smartphone could be exchanged for something delicious?
How can they distinguish objects that humans care about from objects humans barely notice?
And perhaps the most extraordinary question of all:
Have a group of wild monkeys accidentally invented something resembling a primitive economy?
The answer is both simpler and more astonishing than it sounds.

The monkeys at Uluwatu are long-tailed macaques (Macaca fascicularis), also known as crab-eating macaques.
They are widespread across Southeast Asia, inhabiting forests, coastal environments, and landscapes transformed by people.
They are highly adaptable omnivores.
Their diets can include fruit, leaves, seeds, insects, and various other foods.
They also live in complex social groups, where individuals establish relationships, compete over resources, groom one another, and learn from their surroundings.
Uluwatu's macaques are free-ranging animals, not trained performers.
They live around a sacred temple complex where tourists, local staff, religious visitors, and monkeys encounter one another daily.
And therein lies the secret of their extraordinary behavior.
A macaque does not need to understand that a smartphone costs $1,000.
It only needs to notice that humans react very differently when they lose a phone than when they lose an empty plastic wrapper.
One object creates panic.
The other barely attracts attention.
In an environment where people exchange food for recovered belongings, that difference can become extremely valuable information.
Think of it as a strange business school.
The monkeys supply the initiative.
Tourists supply the objects.
Temple staff often facilitate the exchange.
And food becomes the reward.
The monkeys are not selling technology.
They are exploiting a predictable feature of human behavior.
They have learned that an object can be valuable not because they want it, but because someone else desperately wants it back.

The behavior was familiar to local people long before researchers investigated it systematically.
An early account appeared in 1999.
In 2017, primatologist Fany Brotcorne and colleagues published a detailed investigation of robbing and bartering at Uluwatu.
During four months of observation in 2010, researchers recorded 201 robbing-and-bartering events across four neighboring macaque groups.
The researchers noticed important differences between groups.
Some animals engaged in the behavior more frequently than others.
The variation was associated partly with differences in opportunities to interact with tourists.
This suggested that the behavior was not simply an instinct shared equally by all macaques.
Instead, it appeared to be a local tradition.
Then came a more ambitious investigation.
A team led by primatologist Jean-Baptiste Leca studied the monkeys over 273 observation days between September 2015 and August 2016.
The findings, published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2021, provided compelling evidence that experience mattered.
Younger monkeys were generally less skilled at stealing and exchanging objects.
Older animals were more selective.
They were more likely to target objects that humans tended to value highly.
And they showed more sophisticated patterns when deciding which food offers to accept or reject.
Researchers classified objects according to the apparent value humans placed on recovering them.
Phones, wallets, and glasses often ranked higher than comparatively unimportant items.
The monkeys behaved differently depending on these categories.
More experienced individuals were better at retaining valuable objects and obtaining food rewards.
In a separate 2022 study, researchers followed thirteen subadult male macaques for 197 observation hours.
They documented 176 attempted robberies, 92 successful thefts, and 44 exchanges.
Interestingly, social rank was associated with robbery efficiency in one group but not another.
That matters because the behavior cannot be explained by a single rule such as "the strongest monkey gets the best reward."
Experience, opportunity, social relationships, and local circumstances all appear relevant.
The popular description calls the monkeys little negotiators.
The scientific description is more precise.
They have developed a multistep, reward-driven behavior involving object selection, possession, waiting, and exchange.
That is remarkable enough without imagining that they understand contracts, bank balances, or consumer electronics.

Consider two objects.
A cheap hair clip.
And a tourist's prescription glasses.
For the monkey, neither object is edible.
Neither offers obvious nutritional value.
Yet the monkey may receive very different rewards depending on which object it takes.
Why?
Because humans care about them differently.
A tourist who loses a hair clip might shrug.
A tourist who loses prescription glasses may suddenly be unable to see clearly.
The monkey need not understand optics or retail prices.
It needs to learn which possessions produce stronger human efforts to recover them.
This is where the researchers' findings become particularly interesting.
The 2021 study found associations between the relative value of stolen objects and the quantity or quality of food that older monkeys rejected or accepted.
In some situations, experienced monkeys appeared willing to wait or refuse initial offers.
This resembles bargaining.
But is it negotiation in the human sense?
Not necessarily.
Human negotiation involves intentions, expectations, representations of value, and sometimes explicit agreements.
Researchers cannot directly establish that macaques understand all those concepts.
The observed behavior may emerge through learned associations, memory, sensitivity to human reactions, and flexible decision-making.
The monkeys also need not know the difference between ordinary sunglasses and an expensive luxury pair.
They may simply distinguish object categories that regularly produce different rewards.
Still, there is an intriguing parallel with human economics.
Economists distinguish between the usefulness of an object and the value someone assigns to obtaining it.
A bottle of water may be cheap in a supermarket.
In a desert, it can become extraordinarily valuable.
At Uluwatu, a smartphone has little direct value to the monkey.
But its owner may be willing to offer considerable food to recover it.
The macaque has stumbled upon a fundamental feature of exchange:
Value depends not only on the object, but also on how much another individual wants it.
Not bad for an animal that has never attended an economics lecture.

In 1953, scientists studying Japanese macaques on Koshima Island witnessed something remarkable.
A young female monkey named Imo began washing sandy sweet potatoes in water.
Other monkeys gradually adopted similar behavior.
Over time, the practice spread through social relationships and continued across generations.
The Koshima observations became a classic example in the study of animal culture.
There has been debate about exactly how the behavior spread, including the relative importance of imitation, social facilitation, and independent discovery.
But the case transformed how scientists thought about learning in nonhuman animals.
Culture, in a broad biological sense, need not require written language or formal teaching.
It can involve behaviors that persist because individuals acquire them through social influence.
Now consider Uluwatu.
Young macaques observe experienced adults taking objects.
They encounter the human responses that follow.
They experiment.
Some attempts fail.
Others produce food.
Gradually, they improve.
Researchers have observed group-level differences, increased stealing after monkeys witness other thefts, and patterns consistent with long-term social transmission.
The practice appears to have persisted for decades.
But here's a critical detail.
Not every monkey population in Bali has developed the same sophisticated robbing-and-bartering routine.
Even populations living near tourists may behave differently.
That makes Uluwatu particularly interesting.
The monkeys are not merely displaying an ordinary species-wide instinct.
They appear to participate in a local behavioral tradition shaped by their particular environment.
In 2025, an article published in the International Journal of Primatology described the Uluwatu behavior as an example of human–macaque co-construction.
The idea is fascinating.
The monkeys developed their behavior in response to humans.
Humans developed procedures for responding to the monkeys.
Temple staff learned how to retrieve objects.
Tourists learned to guard their valuables—or sometimes failed to.
Over time, the two species established a recurring pattern of interaction.
It is a form of shared behavioral history.
Not a peaceful partnership in every instance.
But certainly more complicated than a monkey randomly stealing someone's sunglasses.
The tourists did not merely enter the monkeys' environment. Together, humans and macaques helped create a new behavioral tradition.

In May 2026, Indian traveler Priti Jain shared a frustrating experience from Uluwatu Temple.
She had purchased a new pair of prescription sunglasses for her holiday.
Within moments of wearing them at the temple, a macaque snatched them.
Jain posted footage showing the animal handling her glasses.
She explained that her prescription was approximately −4 diopters, meaning the loss of corrective eyewear could seriously affect her ability to enjoy the rest of her trip.
Her reaction was far from amused.
She called the monkeys an "absolute menace."
The incident was reported by NDTV and other news outlets.
It illustrates the difference between watching an entertaining monkey video and becoming its unwilling star.
In July 2025, The Wall Street Journal also reported firsthand experiences of tourists losing glasses and phones at Uluwatu.
A visitor described the monkeys as having effectively taken over the temple.
Another said a recovered phone had been damaged.
Then, in September 2026, another video showed monkeys taking sunglasses and a flip-flop.
When someone threw an additional object toward one monkey, the animals moved off with more belongings.
The encounter looked almost like a chaotic comedy.
But it offered a useful reminder.
Wildlife encounters are unpredictable.
A monkey may damage property.
A frightened tourist may fall while chasing an animal.
And a macaque that feels threatened may bite or scratch.
What looks amusing from behind a screen can become a genuine safety problem.
For the animal, meanwhile, repeated conflicts with people can have long-term consequences.

Travel north from Bali to the historic Thai city of Lopburi.
Here, monkeys have become famous for a very different reason.
Large populations of macaques have occupied buildings, streets, and historic sites.
Tourists have long visited to watch and photograph them.
Food provisioning became part of the local interaction.
But as the animals became increasingly accustomed to people, conflicts intensified.
Monkeys entered homes and shops.
Some grabbed food or belongings from residents.
Others became involved in confrontations with pedestrians.
The situation became serious enough for authorities to introduce trapping, relocation, sterilization, and management programmes.
In February 2026, Khaosod Englishreported that Lopburi officials were seeking additional financial support to manage the animals.
The municipality described continuing problems with property damage, attacks, and the costs of housing captured monkeys.
Lopburi's situation is not identical to Uluwatu's.
And not every monkey that approaches humans has learned to barter.
Nevertheless, the comparison reveals the dangers of allowing tourism-driven feeding and close contact to develop without effective management.
When animals repeatedly receive food from people, they can begin treating human spaces as reliable feeding sites.
That may alter their movement, social behavior, and expectations.
Human residents may initially enjoy the wildlife.
Then grow frustrated.
Some may demand removal.
Others may oppose it on animal-welfare grounds.
The result is a difficult conservation problem.
The same behavior that makes a wild animal famous can eventually make it unwelcome.

The Uluwatu macaques are remarkable, but they are not alone in demonstrating flexible learning.
In Japan, generations of macaques have continued food-washing traditions first documented in the 1950s.
In Brazil, bearded capuchin monkeys use tools, including stones, to access food.
A 2024 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examined the spread of new food-extraction techniques among wild capuchins.
The researchers found that social tolerance and attention to successful individuals helped shape the transmission of behavior.
In another experiment published in 2024 in Nature Human Behaviour, chimpanzees learned a complex multistep puzzle after a trained group member demonstrated the solution.
Some individuals acquired a skill they had previously failed to discover independently.
These findings suggest that social learning can allow animals to acquire behaviors beyond what they readily invent alone.
Birds provide another striking example.
New Caledonian crows have demonstrated sophisticated tool-making abilities.
Parrots can learn associations between sounds, objects, and rewards.
Dolphins possess complex social relationships and can acquire behaviors through observation.
Octopuses solve problems and manipulate objects in ways that continue to fascinate researchers.
These abilities do not make every animal intelligent in the same way.
A crow's challenges differ from a dolphin's.
A macaque's social world differs from an octopus's.
And intelligence cannot be summarized by asking which species is closest to behaving like a human.
Evolution has produced many different solutions to different problems.
The Uluwatu monkeys are particularly successful at exploiting a unique opportunity created by tourism.
That is a form of behavioral flexibility.
And flexibility is one of the most valuable qualities an animal can possess in a changing world.

Walk around Uluwatu or parts of Lopburi, and macaques may seem abundant.
They occupy walls.
Cross paths.
Gather around people.
Sometimes they appear to be everywhere.
So it may surprise you to learn that the long-tailed macaque is classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List.
The assessment, published in 2022, reflects concern about long-term population trends and threats that include habitat loss, persecution, and capture for trade.
But this classification has also generated scientific debate.
A 2024 paper questioned whether available population data adequately demonstrated the extent of decline implied by the endangered assessment.
Its authors argued that the species remains highly adaptable and can flourish in human-modified environments.
Other researchers and conservationists emphasize that local abundance does not establish security across a species' entire range.
Both points deserve careful consideration.
A species may be numerous in one city and declining elsewhere.
But conservation claims should also be supported by transparent, reliable population evidence.
The deeper issue is that human–macaque relations are becoming increasingly difficult.
Macaques are intelligent enough to exploit new opportunities.
Humans are changing their habitats rapidly.
And close contact can create conflict, disease risks, and dependence on artificial food sources.
In other words, the monkey that steals your phone is not necessarily thriving simply because it appears clever.
It may be adapting to an environment where human behavior has become an important part of survival.

What to Do If a Monkey Steals Your Phone
Suppose you're visiting Uluwatu and a macaque grabs your belongings.
First, do not panic.
And do not try to grab the object back.
Macaques possess sharp teeth and can bite when frightened or challenged.
Chasing the monkey may increase the risk of injury, particularly near cliff edges or crowded pathways.
Instead, seek help from authorized temple staff.
Local attendants are familiar with the monkeys and often have experience managing retrievals.
If an item is recovered through a food exchange, allow trained or experienced staff to manage the situation rather than attempting your own negotiation.
Do not offer food casually to wild monkeys.
Feeding can reinforce unwanted approaches and increase future conflict.
Better still, prevent the theft in the first place.
Keep your phone in a zipped bag when not needed.
Secure prescription glasses and sunglasses.
Avoid dangling jewelry, loose hats, and open handbags.
Do not carry visible snacks.
Keep children close and give monkeys room to move away.
Avoid direct confrontation and do not attempt to touch or pose with the animals.
If a macaque bites or scratches you, immediately wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water for at least twenty minutes, then seek urgent medical evaluation.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that macaque injuries can expose people to serious infections, including the rare but potentially severe B virus.
Rabies from nonhuman primates is uncommon, but an animal bite still requires professional assessment of rabies risk, wound infection, and tetanus protection.
The safest wildlife encounter is one in which neither the human nor the animal feels threatened.
And sometimes the best photograph is the one you take from a respectful distance.

The monkeys' behavior has become irresistible material for online humor.
People describe them as tiny gangsters.
Four-legged pickpockets.
Tropical business executives.
One can almost imagine a macaque sitting on a temple wall, examining an expensive phone and thinking:
"Excellent. I believe we can discuss terms."
But this humor reveals something interesting about human psychology.
We instinctively interpret animal behavior through familiar human concepts.
A monkey holding an object becomes a hostage-taker.
A monkey refusing a banana becomes a tough negotiator.
A monkey selecting a smartphone becomes a financial genius.
These comparisons are amusing because they resemble human behavior.
But they can also be misleading.
The macaque does not necessarily understand theft as a legal concept.
It does not need to understand ownership rights.
And it is unlikely to appreciate the sentimental value of a tourist's photographs.
Yet scientists do not have to pretend the monkey is a human criminal to recognize its intelligence.
Its ability to learn, remember, discriminate between object categories, and adjust behavior according to reward makes the phenomenon genuinely impressive.
One lesson is especially relevant to humans.
We tend to underestimate how strongly incentives shape behavior.
Offer a reward for a behavior often enough, and that behavior may become more frequent.
This applies to animals.
But it also applies to organizations, businesses, and everyday habits.
If a workplace rewards employees for answering messages at midnight, employees may begin treating permanent availability as normal.
If social media rewards outrage with attention, people may learn to produce more outrage.
If tourists reward monkeys with food after the animals take belongings, some monkeys may learn to take more belongings.
Different situations involve very different mental capacities and motivations.
But the basic importance of consequences is remarkably widespread.
Before asking why an unwanted behavior continues, it is often worth asking what reward is keeping it alive.

For centuries, humans have been fascinated by the differences between ourselves and other animals.
We build cities.
We write books.
We invent money, laws, technology, and complicated economic systems.
Surely, we tell ourselves, that makes human intelligence fundamentally different.
In many important respects, it does.
Human symbolic language, cumulative technology, and social institutions have reached levels of complexity not demonstrated by other species.
But modern animal-cognition research has complicated the idea that intelligence is either fully human or virtually absent.
A monkey does not need to create a stock exchange to demonstrate sensitivity to rewards.
A bird does not need to build a factory to use a tool.
An animal does not need written laws to maintain learned social traditions.
The more researchers investigate natural behavior, the more they discover that other species possess specialized abilities suited to their environments.
The Uluwatu monkeys have developed a particularly unusual strategy.
An object that cannot be eaten becomes useful because of the response it produces in another species.
That is not human commerce.
But it is a clever way of using the surrounding social environment.
And it raises an intriguing philosophical question.
When we describe intelligence, are we measuring how closely another species resembles us?
Or are we measuring how effectively it understands and responds to the world it inhabits?
The second question may be the more revealing one.
Because intelligence is not only about knowing things.
It is also about recognizing opportunities, learning from experience, and adapting when circumstances change.
The macaques of Uluwatu have demonstrated all three.

Return to the cliffside temple.
The sun is setting over the Indian Ocean.
A tourist stands below a stone wall.
Above him sits a macaque, holding something shiny.
The tourist wants the object back.
The monkey appears prepared to wait.
A temple attendant approaches.
Food is offered.
Eventually, the exchange is completed.
The tourist recovers his possession, perhaps slightly damaged and accompanied by an unforgettable story.
The macaque receives something edible.
And both participants continue with their day.
The entire scene seems absurdly human.
There is possession.
There is bargaining.
There is an incentive to cooperate.
And there is a conclusion that leaves both sides with something they value.
But the deeper story is not about a monkey becoming a person.
It is about what happens when two intelligent species share the same environment long enough to influence each other's behavior.
Humans bring technology, tourism, food, and expectations.
Monkeys bring curiosity, memory, social learning, and remarkable adaptability.
Together, they create an interaction neither species could have developed in exactly the same way alone.
The result is fascinating.
Sometimes funny.
Occasionally dangerous.
And deeply revealing.
It reminds us that the natural world is not simply a collection of creatures behaving according to fixed instructions.
Animals learn.
They innovate.
They respond to us.
And our actions can change the opportunities available to them.
The final lesson is therefore about responsibility as much as intelligence.
We can marvel at a monkey that exchanges sunglasses for food.
But we should also ask whether our behavior is encouraging encounters that are safe and sustainable for both species.
We can enjoy wildlife without training it to depend on us.
We can appreciate intelligence without turning animals into performers.
And we can visit extraordinary places without forgetting that we are guests in the lives of the creatures who live there.
As the next tourist reaches for a camera at Uluwatu, somewhere nearby a macaque may already be watching.
Not because it understands the global smartphone market.
Not because it dreams of becoming a millionaire.
But because it has learned a wonderfully effective lesson about human nature.
Sometimes the value of an object lies not in what it can do for you, but in what someone else will give to get it back. https://t.co/VEXdcXrcV8
